context: This promise is spoken in the garden, just after the first sin. The serpent had lied, the man and the woman had eaten, and God was saying what would come of that rebellion. The woman and the serpent are set against each other, and so are their offspring.

Offspring can mean one descendant or a group of descendants. The ESV renders the next clause with the singular pronoun he: the woman's offspring crushes the serpent's head and is wounded. The Westminster Confession 8.6 identifies that offspring with Christ. The verse itself does not name him.
This is still very early. There is no Israel yet, no king, and no Bethlehem. The promise is wide. Later promises will name a family, a tribe, a town, and at last a person.

passages.text: I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring; he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel.

connections.text: Galatians 4:4 says that God sent his Son, born of woman. That birth statement is explicit. Galatians does not quote Genesis 3:15 or call the birth its fulfillment. The Westminster Confession 8.6 identifies Christ as the woman's offspring, and Romans 16:20 speaks of Satan being crushed. This is a confessional Reformed reading built from those texts, not a direct fulfillment formula in Galatians.

The line to Abraham is marked typology, not a link the New Testament spells out in one sentence. Some faithful readers see one promise getting narrower: the child who crushes the serpent will come through Abraham's family. Others stay cautious, because Genesis never says that Genesis 3:15 and Genesis 22:18 are the same promise. Both readings can honor the text. The map does not pretend the link is a quotation.

nt: The New Testament does not quote Genesis 3:15 as a fulfillment formula. It says God sent his Son, born of woman (Galatians 4:4), and that the Son shared our flesh and blood to destroy the devil (Hebrews 2:14). Romans 16:20 says God will soon crush Satan under his people's feet. Revelation 12 pictures the ancient serpent at war with the woman and her offspring. The Westminster Confession 8.6 therefore identifies Christ as the woman's offspring while the map labels the link to Abraham as interpretive.
questions: What has just happened in the garden when God speaks this promise?
Who is hurt in the promise, and who is crushed?
Why might a careful reader say this points to Jesus, and why might another reader want a later verse before saying so?

context: Abraham lives long after the garden. God calls him to leave his country, promises him a family, and later tests him on a mountain. Genesis 22 is the story of Isaac, the son Abraham was told to offer. God provides a ram, and then repeats the promise.

Genesis speaks of Abraham's offspring, a word that can refer to descendants collectively. Through that offspring, every nation will be blessed. Paul later identifies the offspring with Christ in Galatians 3:16. The story of Israel, the kings, and Jesus grows inside this family promise.

A covenant is a binding relationship God establishes, with promises and obligations. God's covenant dealings with Abraham do not replace the garden promise. In the Reformed reading used by this map, they make the older hope more specific.

passages.text: and in your offspring shall all the nations of the earth be blessed, because you have obeyed my voice.

connections.text: The line back to the first promise is interpretive. Some readers see Abraham's offspring as the next step of the child promised in the garden. Others note that Genesis itself does not join the two verses. In the Reformed reading used here, the two promises are read together as stages in the hope that reaches Christ.

The line to Jesus is explicit at the level of the Abrahamic promises. Paul says the promises were made to Abraham and his offspring, who is Christ (Galatians 3:16). Matthew 1:1 calls Jesus the son of Abraham. Galatians does not identify Genesis 22:18 by verse number, so the claim should not be narrower than Paul's wording.

nt: Paul identifies the offspring in the Abrahamic promises with Christ (Galatians 3:16). He also calls those who belong to Christ Abraham's offspring (Galatians 3:29), so the word can still have a collective use. Those who trust Christ are Abraham's children by faith (Galatians 3:7-9, 14). Peter quotes the promise that all families will be blessed and says God sent his servant to bless his hearers (Acts 3:25-26). Jesus says Abraham rejoiced that he would see his day (John 8:56).
questions: What did God promise Abraham's offspring would do for the nations?
How does Paul identify Abraham's offspring in Galatians 3:16, and how does he use the word again in Galatians 3:29?
What is the difference between a link the New Testament states and a link we notice by reading two Old Testament promises together?

context: Jacob is dying in Egypt. He calls his sons and speaks a word over each one. Judah is the fourth son, not the oldest. Jacob does not give the ruler's place to Reuben, Simeon, or Levi. He gives it to Judah.

A scepter is a king's staff. Jacob says that the scepter will not depart from Judah until tribute comes to its ruler, and that the peoples will obey him. The promise of offspring is now joined to royal rule in one tribe.
This is still centuries before David. The family is not yet a nation with a throne. The word stands over a tribe, waiting for a son who will hold the rule.

passages.text: The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor the ruler’s staff from between his feet, until tribute comes to him; and to him shall be the obedience of the peoples.

connections.text: The line to Jesus is explicit. An elder in Revelation calls him the Lion of the tribe of Judah (Revelation 5:5). Hebrews 7:14 says it is clear that our Lord descended from Judah. The New Testament itself places Jesus in that tribe.

The line to David follows the family. Ruth 4:18-22 lists the names from Perez, Judah's son, down to David. Matthew 1:3-6 repeats that family list. The New Testament genealogy states the path from Judah's house to David's throne.

nt: Revelation 5:5 is worship language. The Lion of Judah has conquered, and he is also the Root of David. Hebrews uses Judah for a different point, about priests, but it states the family fact plainly: our Lord descended from Judah. Matthew's opening genealogy begins the same story in a list of names, from Abraham to Judah to David to Joseph (Matthew 1:1-16).
questions: Why is it striking that the ruler's promise goes to Judah, not the oldest son?
What does a scepter stand for in this blessing?
Which New Testament verses say Jesus belongs to Judah, and what do they add besides the family name?

context: Isaiah speaks when David's royal tree looks cut down. Kings have failed. Enemies threaten. The prophet does not say God is finished with Jesse's family. Jesse is David's father, from Bethlehem. Isaiah sees a shoot from the stump, and a branch from the roots.

The picture is a tree cut to the ground that starts to grow again. The new growth is a king. The Spirit of the Lord rests on him. He judges with righteousness. Later in the same chapter, the root of Jesse stands as a signal, and the nations come to him.
This prophecy looks back to the promise to Judah and to God's earlier covenant with David. The family is named again through Jesse, David's father.

passages.text: There shall come forth a shoot from the stump of Jesse, and a branch from his roots shall bear fruit.

connections.text: The line to Jesus is explicit. Paul quotes Isaiah on the root of Jesse and says the Gentiles will hope in him (Romans 15:12). The New Testament itself reads that prophecy as a word about Christ, and about nations hoping in him.

nt: Romans 15:12 is a quotation, not a loose hint. Paul is teaching Jewish and Gentile believers to welcome one another, and he piles up Scriptures about the nations. Isaiah's root of Jesse is one of them. Revelation 5:5 and Revelation 22:16 also call Jesus the Root of David. The family name and the nations belong together in the New Testament reading.
questions: What does a stump suggest about David's family at the time Isaiah speaks?
What does Paul say the nations will do because of the root of Jesse?
How is a root both the start of a tree and, in this title, the king the nations look for?

context: David is king in Jerusalem and wants to build a house for God. God answers through the prophet Nathan by promising to establish David's house and to raise up a son who will build a house for God's name.

God promises an offspring from David's own body. That son will build a house for God's name. His throne will be made sure forever. This covenant is God's binding commitment concerning a son and a kingdom that does not end.

David's own son Solomon builds the temple, and the kingdom later splits and falls. In the Christian canonical reading, the word forever reaches beyond Solomon to a son whose reign does not end. Luke 1:32-33 and Acts 2:30-32 identify that hope with Jesus.

passages.text: When your days are fulfilled and you lie down with your fathers, I will raise up your offspring after you, who shall come from your body, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever.
And your house and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before me. Your throne shall be established forever.

connections.text: The line from Judah is the family behind David. Ruth 4:18-22 and Matthew 1:3-6 list the generations. The New Testament genealogy treats David's throne as the throne that grew inside Judah's family.

The line to Gabriel's announcement is explicit. The angel tells Mary that the Lord God will give her son the throne of his father David, and that his kingdom will have no end (Luke 1:32-33). The New Testament itself puts David's forever promise on Jesus.

The line to Joseph follows the family record. Matthew 1:6-16 lists the names from David to Joseph, and the angel calls Joseph son of David (Matthew 1:20). The New Testament itself gives Joseph that title and that genealogy.

The line to Bethlehem is about place. God sends Samuel to Jesse the Bethlehemite to find a king among his sons (1 Samuel 16:1). Luke 2:4 calls Bethlehem the city of David, because Joseph is of David's house. The New Testament itself ties the town to David.

nt: Luke 1:32-33 is the plain New Testament reading of this covenant. The son promised to Mary receives David's throne, and the kingdom does not end. Peter, preaching at Pentecost, says David was a prophet and knew God had sworn to set one of his descendants on his throne (Acts 2:30). The apostles do not leave the promise with Solomon.
questions: What did David want to build, and what did God promise to build instead?
Why is the word forever too big for Solomon alone?
Where does the angel use David's promise, almost in David's own words?

context: Isaiah speaks this sign to Ahaz, king of Judah, in a time of war. Two kings are threatening Jerusalem. God tells Ahaz to ask for a sign. Ahaz refuses, and God gives a sign anyway.

The sign is a child called Immanuel. Isaiah ties the sign to a near timetable: before the child knows how to refuse evil and choose good, the two threatening kings will be deserted. Interpreters differ about the child's identity in Isaiah's own day. The name means God with us.

The map does not flatten the history. Ahaz had a crisis. Matthew, centuries later, says the birth of Jesus fulfills what the prophet spoke. Christians read both the moment in Isaiah's day and the fuller fulfillment in Jesus.

passages.text: Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.

connections.text: The line to the birth is explicit. Matthew says all this took place to fulfill what the Lord spoke by the prophet, and he quotes Isaiah 7:14 (Matthew 1:22-23). The New Testament itself identifies the virgin's son, Immanuel, with the child born to Mary.

nt: Matthew does not merely mention the name. He quotes the sentence and then translates it. Isaiah says the child shall be called Immanuel. Matthew says they shall call his name Immanuel, which means God with us (Matthew 1:23). The quotation is the New Testament's reading of the sign. In the Christian canonical reading, the child conceived by the Holy Spirit is God come to be with his people.
questions: What trouble was Ahaz facing when Isaiah spoke of a sign?
What does Matthew add when he quotes Isaiah, besides the name itself?
Why does the meaning God with us matter for who Jesus is, not only for what he is called?

word_study.text: Matthew 1:23 gives the meaning in plain words: God with us. The Hebrew combines a word meaning with, the suffix us, and El, meaning God. The Gospel supplies the translation, so no proposed hidden meaning is needed.

context: Isaiah 9 follows a dark word about the land. People are walking in gloom. Then the prophet says a light has shone. The joy is compared to a harvest and to the day Midian was beaten. The boots of soldiers and the garments rolled in blood are burned.

The reason for the joy is a child. A child is born, a son is given, and the government rests on his shoulder. His names are Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace. His government and peace do not end. He sits on David's throne.

This prophecy was spoken centuries before Jesus. It gathers the king promise into one child whose titles include Mighty God and who reigns from David's throne. Matthew applies Isaiah 9:1-2 to Jesus, while Luke 1:32-33 parallels the throne promise in Isaiah 9:7.

passages.text: For to us a child is born, to us a son is given; and the government shall be upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace.

connections.text: The line to Jesus is explicit because of Matthew 4:13-16. Matthew quotes Isaiah 9:1-2, the people in darkness seeing a great light, and says this is fulfilled when Jesus begins his work in Galilee. The New Testament itself uses that part of the chapter for him. Isaiah 9:6-7 is the next part of the same prophecy, the child on David's throne. Matthew does not quote those verses in chapter 4. Readers connect them to Jesus because of the quotation he does make, and because Gabriel promised Mary's son the throne of David (Luke 1:32-33).

nt: Be careful and clear. Matthew quotes Isaiah 9:1-2, not Isaiah 9:6, in Matthew 4:15-16. The light in Galilee is the sentence he marks as fulfilled. The child who is born, and the names that follow, belong to the same oracle. Luke 1:32-33 says Jesus will reign on David's throne forever, which is what Isaiah 9:7 says about this child's kingdom. That is how the New Testament gives you the pieces, and how Christians put them together.
questions: Which verses of Isaiah 9 does Matthew quote, and where?
What throne does Isaiah give this child, and who else is promised that throne?
Why is it honest to say Matthew uses Isaiah 9 of Jesus, and also honest to say he does not quote the line about the child in that place?

context: Micah prophesies when Assyria is a terror and Judah's rulers are failing. He speaks judgment, and he also speaks hope. The hope is not a bigger city. It is a small clan town, Bethlehem Ephrathah.

God speaks to the town. From you will come a ruler in Israel. The town is too little to be counted among the clans, and yet the ruler comes from there. Micah also says this ruler will stand and shepherd his flock in the strength of the Lord.
Bethlehem is already known as David's town. The prophecy does not invent a new place. It says the next ruler comes from the old king's hometown.

passages.text: But you, O Bethlehem Ephrathah, who are too little to be among the clans of Judah, from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel, whose coming forth is from of old, from ancient days.

connections.text: The line to the town is the prophecy's own address. Micah speaks to Bethlehem Ephrathah. The place on the map is that town. The link is the name the prophet uses.

The line to the birth is explicit. Matthew 2:4-6 says Herod asked where the Christ was to be born, and the chief priests and scribes answered with Micah's words about Bethlehem. The New Testament itself cites the prophecy for Jesus' birthplace.

nt: Matthew 2:6 quotes the sense of Micah 5:2 and even sharpens the town's honor: you are by no means least among the rulers of Judah, for from you shall come a ruler who will shepherd my people Israel. John 7:42 shows that people in Jesus' day already expected the Christ to come from Bethlehem, the village of David. The New Testament both quotes the prophet and shows that Israel knew the expectation.
questions: Why does Micah stress that Bethlehem is little?
Who quotes Micah when Herod asks where the king will be born?
What does the ruler do for the flock, according to Micah 5?

context: Bethlehem is a town in Judah near Jerusalem, not the capital. Ruth's story opens with a family from Bethlehem who leave during a famine. Ruth later returns with Naomi, and Ruth's son Obed becomes the grandfather of David.
Samuel later goes to Bethlehem to anoint a king from Jesse's sons. The youngest, David, is keeping sheep. The town is David's hometown, and Luke calls it the city of David.

The Hebrew name is commonly translated house of bread. Beth means house, and lehem means bread. This well-attested meaning is not, by itself, a prophecy. The town matters on this map because of David, Micah, and the birth of Jesus.

passages.text: And Joseph also went up from Galilee, from the town of Nazareth, to Judea, to the city of David, which is called Bethlehem, because he was of the house and lineage of David, to be registered with Mary, his betrothed, who was with child.

connections.text: The line from Micah's prophecy is the prophet speaking to this town by name. Micah 5:2 says the ruler comes from Bethlehem Ephrathah.

The line from David's covenant is the place of his family. Samuel is sent to Jesse the Bethlehemite (1 Samuel 16:1). Luke 2:4 says Joseph must go to Bethlehem because he is of David's house. The New Testament itself calls the town the city of David.
The line to the birth is the event in the town. Luke 2:4-7 says they travel to Bethlehem and the child is born there, laid in a manger because there is no place for them where they are staying.

nt: Luke 2:4-7 is the New Testament's account of the town at the birth. Matthew 2:1 says Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea. Matthew 2:5-6 adds the scribes' quotation of Micah. John 7:42 shows the public expectation that the Christ comes from Bethlehem, David's village.
questions: What stories, before Jesus, already tie Bethlehem to David?
Why does Joseph go there in Luke 2?
What is the difference between a meaning of a town's name and a promise God makes?

word_study.text: The Hebrew name is commonly translated house of bread. Beth means house, and lehem means bread. The name does not make Jesus' words in John 6:35 a prophecy. Matthew and Luke connect the town to David and Micah, not to the bread of life saying.

context: Mary is a virgin in Nazareth, pledged to be married to Joseph. Luke introduces her when God sends the angel Gabriel to her.

Gabriel says she has found favor with God. She will conceive and bear a son, and she will call him Jesus. He will be great, the Son of the Most High, and he will receive the throne of David. Mary asks how this can be, since she is a virgin. The angel says the Holy Spirit will come upon her.

Mary's answer is trust. She calls herself the servant of the Lord and asks that the word be done to her. She is the mother of Jesus. The Gospels do not turn her into a savior. They honor her faith and her place in the birth.

passages.text: And behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus.

connections.text: The line from the announcement is the order of the story. Gabriel's words are spoken to Mary. Luke 1:26-38 tells the visit, her question, and her yes. The New Testament itself joins the announcement to her.

The line to the birth is explicit. Luke 2:7 says she gave birth to her firstborn son, wrapped him in swaddling cloths, and laid him in a manger. She is his mother in the narrative the New Testament tells.

nt: Matthew 1:18-25 tells the same conception from Joseph's side and quotes Isaiah's virgin. Luke tells it from Mary's side. Paul says God sent his Son, born of woman (Galatians 4:4). The New Testament is consistent: Jesus has a human mother, and the child is conceived by the Holy Spirit, not by an ordinary father.
questions: What does Gabriel promise Mary about her son's throne?
How does Mary answer, and what does that answer show?
What do Luke, Matthew, and Paul each say about Jesus being born of a woman?

context: Joseph is a descendant of David, engaged to Mary. When he learns she is expecting a child, he is a just man and plans to divorce her quietly rather than shame her.

An angel appears in a dream and calls him son of David. The child conceived in Mary is from the Holy Spirit. Joseph is to take Mary as his wife and name the son Jesus, because he will save his people from their sins.

Joseph obeys and takes Mary as his wife. He is not Jesus' biological father. Matthew's genealogy ends with Joseph, and Joseph names the child. Christian interpreters commonly describe this role as legal fatherhood, but Matthew does not use that legal phrase.

passages.text: Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary as your wife, for that which is conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit.

connections.text: Matthew 1:6-16 traces the genealogy from David to Joseph, and the angel calls Joseph son of David (Matthew 1:20). This places Joseph in David's line. The text does not call the relationship legal fatherhood, though Christian interpreters commonly use that phrase for Joseph's role.

Matthew 1:16 calls Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born. Matthew 1:25 says Joseph named the child, while Matthew 1:20 says the child was conceived by the Holy Spirit. Joseph's fatherhood is not biological. Describing it as legal fatherhood is a standard inference from the genealogy and naming, not a phrase Matthew uses.

nt: Matthew traces David's line to Joseph, calls him son of David, and records that he named the child Jesus. Luke 2:4 says Joseph goes to Bethlehem because he is of David's house and lineage. The Gospels also state that Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit. Christian interpreters commonly call Joseph Jesus' legal father, but the Gospels do not use that legal term.
questions: What was Joseph planning to do before the dream, and why?
What two things does the angel tell him about the child's origin and name?
Why does Matthew trace a genealogy to Joseph if Joseph is not the biological father?

context: The annunciation is Gabriel's visit to Mary in Nazareth, in the sixth month of Elizabeth's pregnancy. God sends the angel. This is not a vague feeling. It is a message with a child, a name, and a throne.
The son will be called the Son of the Most High. The Lord God will give him the throne of his father David. He will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and his kingdom will have no end.
Mary asks how, because she is a virgin. Gabriel answers that the Holy Spirit will come upon her and the power of the Most High will overshadow her. The child will be called holy, the Son of God.

passages.text: He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High. And the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.

connections.text: The line from David's covenant is the throne in the angel's sentence. Luke 1:32-33 takes the forever kingdom promised to David's offspring and speaks it over Mary's son. The New Testament itself makes that connection.
The line to Mary is the order of the event. The announcement happens to her. Luke 1:26-38 is one scene: the angel comes, Mary hears, Mary responds. The New Testament tells it that way.

nt: Luke 1:32-33 is the New Testament reading of the Davidic promise at the moment of the announcement. The throne, the house of Jacob, and the kingdom without end are Gabriel's words, not a later guess. Matthew 1:20-23 tells the matching announcement to Joseph and adds Isaiah's Immanuel. Together the Gospels say the child is David's heir and God with us, conceived by the Holy Spirit.
questions: What three things does Gabriel say about the son's kingdom?
What question does Mary ask, and what does the answer protect?
Which older promise sounds most like the angel's words about the throne?

context: Luke reports that Caesar ordered a registration. Joseph goes from Nazareth to Bethlehem because he belongs to David's house. Mary, who is expecting, goes with him. While they are there, the time comes, and she gives birth.

The child is laid in a manger because there is no place for them where they are staying. That night, angels tell shepherds in the fields that a Savior has been born in the city of David. He is Christ the Lord. The shepherds go and find the baby.

Matthew tells the same birth from another side. Mary is found to be with child by the Holy Spirit. The angel tells Joseph. The birth fulfills Isaiah's word about the virgin and Immanuel. Later, wise men come, and the scribes point Herod to Bethlehem.

passages.text: For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Savior, who is Christ the Lord.
And she gave birth to her firstborn son and wrapped him in swaddling cloths and laid him in a manger, because there was no place for them in the inn.

connections.text: The line from the first promise uses Galatians 4:4. God sent his Son, born of a woman. The New Testament states the birth. It does not quote Genesis 3:15 in that verse. Christians also hear the garden promise fulfilled in this child, and the confession says the seed of the woman is Christ. The cited New Testament line for the birth is Galatians 4:4.
The line from Immanuel is Matthew's quotation. He says the birth fulfills Isaiah 7:14, and he translates the name as God with us (Matthew 1:22-23). The New Testament itself makes that link.
The line from Mary is the birth narrative. Luke 2:7 says she gave birth to her firstborn son. The New Testament tells you who the mother is.
The line from Micah is the scribes' answer to Herod. Matthew 2:4-6 quotes the prophet and names Bethlehem as the place of the king's birth. The New Testament itself uses Micah for this event.
The line from the town is Luke's travel note and birth. Luke 2:4-7 says they go to Bethlehem, the city of David, and the child is born there.

nt: Luke gives the angel's sentence: a Savior, Christ the Lord, in the city of David (Luke 2:11). Matthew gives Isaiah and the name Immanuel (Matthew 1:22-23), and the scribes' use of Micah (Matthew 2:4-6). Paul gives the simple fact that the Son was born of woman when the time was full (Galatians 4:4). The New Testament reads this birth as the arrival of the promised person, not as one more story in a list.
questions: Why is Jesus born in Bethlehem, according to Luke?
What three titles does the angel give the child in Luke 2:11?
Which prophet does Matthew quote, and which prophet do the scribes quote?

context: Matthew begins his Gospel with a genealogy, not a definition. The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham. In one line he sets Jesus inside the two great family promises, Abraham's offspring and David's king.

Christ is not a last name. It is the Greek title corresponding to Messiah, and both mean Anointed One. In this story, Jesus is the promised king. His personal name is Jesus, the name Joseph is told to give because he will save his people from their sins.

Every other stop on this map is a thread. This stop is the person the threads are for. He is the son in the promises, the king from Judah and Jesse and David, the child of Mary, the one born in Bethlehem, and the one who says he gives life.

passages.text: The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham.
She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins.

connections.text: The line from Abraham is explicit. Paul says the offspring in Abraham's promise is Christ (Galatians 3:16). Matthew 1:1 calls Jesus the son of Abraham. The New Testament itself names him as that descendant.
The line from Judah is explicit. Revelation 5:5 calls him the Lion of the tribe of Judah. Hebrews 7:14 says our Lord descended from Judah. The New Testament itself gives him that tribe.
The line from Jesse is explicit. Paul quotes Isaiah about the root of Jesse and says the nations will hope in him (Romans 15:12). The New Testament itself applies the prophecy to Christ.

The line from Joseph follows Matthew's genealogy to Joseph, calls him Mary's husband, and records that Joseph named Jesus (Matthew 1:16, 20, 25). Christian interpreters commonly describe this as legal fatherhood, but Matthew does not use that phrase. Matthew also states the miraculous conception.

The line from Isaiah's child uses Matthew 4:13-16, where Isaiah 9:1-2 is fulfilled in Jesus' ministry in Galilee. The child on David's throne in Isaiah 9:6-7 is read with Luke 1:32-33. The New Testament quote in Matthew is Isaiah 9:1-2. The throne promise is Gabriel's word.

The line from the wise men is the scene in Matthew 2. They ask for the one born king of the Jews, and they worship the child (Matthew 2:2, Matthew 2:11). The New Testament itself shows them coming to Jesus.

nt: The New Testament reads the whole line of promises as ending on this person. Matthew 1:1 stacks Abraham and David on his name. Luke 2:11 calls the baby Savior, Christ the Lord. John 1:41 has Andrew say he has found the Messiah, and John explains that Messiah means Christ. Galatians 3:16 says the offspring is Christ. The Gospels and Paul are not telling unrelated stories. They are naming one man.
questions: What two ancestors does Matthew put in his first sentence, and why those two?
What is the difference between the name Jesus and the title Christ?
Which of the lines into this stop is a quotation of an Old Testament promise, and which is a family record?

word_study.text: John 1:41 gives the translation. Andrew says, We have found the Messiah, and John adds, which means Christ. Messiah comes from a Hebrew word meaning anointed one, and Christ is the corresponding Greek title. In Israel, kings and priests were anointed. The Westminster Standards describe Christ as the anointed prophet, priest, and king.

context: After Jesus is born in Bethlehem, wise men from the east arrive in Jerusalem. They have seen a star. They ask a public question: where is he who has been born king of the Jews?

Herod is troubled, and all Jerusalem with him. He gathers the chief priests and scribes. They answer from the prophet: Bethlehem. Herod sends the wise men, pretending he wants to worship too. The star leads them to the house. They see the child with Mary, fall down, and worship. They offer gold, frankincense, and myrrh, and they go home another way.

Matthew does not identify the wise men's ethnicity. Because they travel from the east outside Judea, they are commonly read as Gentiles. Their visit fits Matthew's wider theme of the nations coming to Israel's king, but Matthew does not call it a fulfillment of the promise to Abraham or quote a prophecy about their gifts.

passages.text: Where is he who has been born king of the Jews? For we saw his star when it rose and have come to worship him.

connections.text: The line to Jesus is explicit. Matthew 2:2 records their question about the child born king. Matthew 2:11 records that they worshiped him. The New Testament itself shows the search ending on Jesus, not on a symbol.

nt: Matthew's own reading of the visit includes the scribes' use of Micah 5:2. The king the nations seek is the ruler from Bethlehem. The story does not quote Genesis or Isaiah 60 as a fulfillment formula. Those older poems about kings bringing gifts are passages Christians sometimes set beside this scene. Matthew's stated quotation is the Bethlehem prophecy. The stated action is worship of the child.
questions: What do the wise men call the child before they ever see him?
Who tells them the town, and which prophet do they use?
What do they do when they find the child, and what does their worship say about the child they found in a house?

context: This saying comes later than the birth, in Jesus' public ministry. A crowd has eaten bread he provided. They follow him to the other side of the sea. Jesus tells them they are seeking him because they ate their fill, not because they saw what the sign meant.

He tells them to work for food that endures to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give. They ask for a sign like the manna in the wilderness. Jesus says the true bread from heaven is the one the Father gives. Then he says the sentence: I am the bread of life.
John 6:35 sets coming to him and believing in him alongside the promises of no hunger and no thirst. The bread is not a town and not a loaf. It is Jesus himself.

passages.text: Jesus said to them, “I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst.”

nt: Jesus explains the sentence in the same chapter. John 6:35 places coming to him and believing in him alongside the promise of no hunger and no thirst. He also says that everyone who looks on the Son and believes has eternal life (John 6:40). He compares himself with the manna (John 6:31-33). Bethlehem is not part of his explanation.
questions: What had the crowd just received, and what does Jesus say they should seek instead?
How does Jesus define not hungering and not thirsting?
Which connections does Jesus himself make in John 6?

context: Isaiah 1:1 sets his work in Judah, in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. That is four kings. Assyria is rising through those years. Under Ahaz the pressure comes to a head, and Ahaz answers it by paying Assyria to protect him rather than trusting the Lord.

Isaiah 6 tells how he was called. He sees the Lord, he says he is a man of unclean lips, and a coal from the altar touches his mouth. His guilt is taken away first, and then he is sent. What he is sent to do is speak, and he is told plainly that many will not listen. The prophet's part is the message. The outcome belongs to God.

Three stops on this map are sentences from his book. Ahaz is offered a sign and turns it down, and a sign is given anyway, the son called Immanuel. A child is born for us and the government rests on his shoulder. A shoot comes up from a stump, the stump of Jesse, and the nations seek that root.

connections.text: The sign of Immanuel is Isaiah 7:14, a verse in Isaiah's own book. Matthew 1:22-23 quotes it and says this took place to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet. Matthew does not name Isaiah in that verse, though he names him in other places.

This stop is Isaiah 9:1-7. Matthew 4:14-16 names Isaiah and quotes the opening of it, Isaiah 9:1-2, about the light in Galilee. The child in Isaiah 9:6-7 is not quoted there, so the New Testament names the prophet of this passage without quoting that verse.
The shoot from Jesse's stump is Isaiah 11:1. Paul quotes Isaiah 11:10 at Romans 15:12 and says Isaiah is the one who says it. That is the New Testament naming the prophet and the verse together.

nt: The New Testament names Isaiah often. Matthew 3:3 says John the Baptist is the one spoken of by the prophet Isaiah, quoting Isaiah 40:3. Matthew 4:14 names him when quoting Isaiah 9:1-2. Romans 15:12 introduces a quotation of Isaiah 11:10 with the words Isaiah says. John 12:38-41 quotes Isaiah twice and says Isaiah spoke of Christ because he had seen his glory.
questions: What is Isaiah sent to do in Isaiah 6, and what is he not promised?
Ahaz is offered a sign and refuses it. What happens next?
Which of these three sayings does the New Testament tie to Isaiah by name, and which one does it leave to the prophet without naming him?

context: Israel has been out of Egypt for forty years. The people are camped in Moab, east of the Jordan, with the land in front of them. Moses will not cross over with them. He dies in Moab at the end of the book.

The English name Deuteronomy comes from the Greek title of the book, which means second law. It is not a second, different law. It is Moses going back over the law God had already given, explaining it to the people before they go in.
Almost all of what follows is Moses speaking. The book records the sermon, and the last chapter tells how he died.

passages.text: These are the words that Moses spoke to all Israel beyond the Jordan in the wilderness, in the Arabah opposite Suph, between Paran and Tophel, Laban, Hazeroth, and Dizahab.
Beyond the Jordan, in the land of Moab, Moses undertook to explain this law

nt: The New Testament treats this book as the words of Moses and quotes it often. Jesus uses it three times in the wilderness and once when asked about the greatest commandment. Peter, Stephen, and Paul all quote it. The book's opening sentences are not among the verses they quote, which is why this stop has no line on the map. The stops after it do.
questions: Where is Israel standing when Moses begins to speak?
What does it mean that Moses undertook to explain the law rather than give a new one?
Why might a last sermon sound different from a first one?

context: Moses repeats the ten commandments that God gave at Horeb, the mountain also called Sinai. The people had heard them there. He says them again here, before they cross the Jordan.

Notice where he starts. Before a single command there is a sentence about what God has done. I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. The commands come after the rescue, not before it.
Then the ten follow, from having no other gods to not wanting what belongs to a neighbor.

passages.text: I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.
You shall have no other gods before me.

And you shall not covet your neighbor’s wife. And you shall not desire your neighbor’s house, his field, or his male servant, or his female servant, his ox, or his donkey, or anything that is your neighbor’s.

connections.text: The link runs through Deuteronomy 5:31, where God tells Moses he will give him the whole commandment and the statutes and the rules to teach. Deuteronomy 6:1 picks up those same three terms as Moses begins to teach them. Read 6:1 carefully: it introduces what is coming rather than pointing back at the ten words. The join between the two chapters is in the book's own words, and the site does not quote 6:1 because the ESV sets it with em dashes.

nt: None of the verses on this map are quoted out of chapter 5. The chapter that follows it is quoted three times. What chapter 5 gives the reader is the ground the rest of the sermon stands on: a God who rescued first, then commanded.
questions: What does God say about himself before he gives a single command?
Why might the order matter, rescue first and commands after?
Which of the ten would a person be able to break without anyone else noticing?

context: This is the passage Jewish readers call the Shema, after its first word in Hebrew: hear. Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one.

What follows is a command to love God with everything a person is. Heart, soul, might. Then instructions for ordinary life. Teach these words to your children. Talk about them when you sit at home and when you walk down the road, when you lie down and when you get up. Write them on your doorposts.

Two more verses in this chapter matter for the map. Fear the LORD and serve him, and swear by his name (6:13). Do not put him to the test (6:16). Jesus used both of those in the wilderness, and he used verse 5 when a lawyer asked him which commandment was greatest.

passages.text: Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one.
You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might.
It is the LORD your God you shall fear. Him you shall serve and by his name you shall swear.
You shall not put the LORD your God to the test, as you tested him at Massah.

connections.text: The link runs through Deuteronomy 5:31, where God tells Moses he will give him the whole commandment and the statutes and the rules to teach. Deuteronomy 6:1 picks up those same three terms as Moses begins to teach them. Read 6:1 carefully: it introduces what is coming rather than pointing back at the ten words. The join between the two chapters is in the book's own words, and the site does not quote 6:1 because the ESV sets it with em dashes.

Two of Jesus' three answers in the wilderness come from this chapter, and both are introduced with the words it is written. Matthew 4:7 quotes Deuteronomy 6:16 almost word for word. Matthew 4:10 reads 'You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve', where Deuteronomy 6:13 reads 'It is the LORD your God you shall fear. Him you shall serve'. Worship stands where Deuteronomy has fear, and the word only is added. The quotation is marked either way.

Jesus quotes verse 5 and calls it the great and first commandment (Matthew 22:37-38). Matthew reads 'with all your mind' where Deuteronomy reads 'with all your might'. Mark has four terms, heart, soul, mind, and strength (Mark 12:30), and Mark also keeps verse 4 about the Lord being one. Neither Gospel comments on the difference in wording.

Chapters 6 to 8 are one continuous address. Deuteronomy 8:1 resumes 'The whole commandment that I command you today', the same formula used at 5:31 and again at 7:11. That makes this a link inside one sermon rather than a back reference to chapter 6 in particular. It is not a quotation and not a prophecy.

nt: Jesus quotes this chapter more than any other part of Deuteronomy. Twice to the devil, from verses 16 and 13, and once to a lawyer, from verse 5. Luke reports the same two wilderness answers in a different order (Luke 4:8, 4:12). Mark 12:29 keeps the sentence about God being one in front of the command to love him, which is how Deuteronomy has it.
questions: What does the passage ask a person to love God with?
Where does it say these words should be talked about?
Jesus answered a test with verse 16, which is about testing God. What do you make of that?

context: Moses looks back over the forty years. He says God led them, humbled them, and tested them, to know what was in their heart and whether they would keep his commandments (8:2).
The manna is part of the test. They were hungry, and God fed them with bread they had never seen before, so that they would learn where life comes from. Man does not live by bread alone.
Verse 5 gives the reason in a sentence a child could follow. As a man disciplines his son, the LORD your God disciplines you.

passages.text: And you shall remember the whole way that the LORD your God has led you these forty years in the wilderness, that he might humble you, testing you to know what was in your heart, whether you would keep his commandments or not.
that man does not live by bread alone, but man lives by every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD.
Know then in your heart that, as a man disciplines his son, the LORD your God disciplines you.

connections.text: Chapters 6 to 8 are one continuous address. Deuteronomy 8:1 resumes 'The whole commandment that I command you today', the same formula used at 5:31 and again at 7:11. That makes this a link inside one sermon rather than a back reference to chapter 6 in particular. It is not a quotation and not a prophecy.

Jesus says it is written and quotes this verse when the devil tells him to make bread (Matthew 4:4). The citation is explicit. Matthew reads 'the mouth of God' where Deuteronomy reads 'the mouth of the LORD'. Many readers also set the two scenes side by side, Israel tested forty years and Jesus tested forty days. Matthew does not state that comparison in so many words. What he states is the quotation.

nt: Jesus quotes verse 3 in the wilderness, hungry, after forty days without food (Matthew 4:1-4). Luke's version keeps only the first half of the sentence: Man shall not live by bread alone (Luke 4:4). Matthew keeps the whole of it, including the words about every word from the mouth of God, which is the part Deuteronomy is making its point with.
questions: What does Moses say the hunger and the manna were for?
What is the difference between living on bread and living on God's word?
Jesus had gone forty days without food when he quoted this. Does that change how you read it?

context: At Horeb the people had asked not to hear God's voice directly again, because the fire and the voice frightened them (18:16). God answers that request by promising a prophet.

The prophet will be like Moses and will come from among their own brothers. God says he will put his words in that prophet's mouth, and the prophet will speak all that God commands (18:18). Israel is told to listen. Whoever will not listen to those words will answer to God himself (18:19).
The promise is singular in form. Israel did have many prophets after Moses, and some readers take the promise as covering that whole line. The apostles apply it to one person.

passages.text: The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you, from your brothers
I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers. And I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I command him.
And whoever will not listen to my words that he shall speak in my name, I myself will require it of him.

connections.text: Peter quotes this promise at the temple, names Moses as the one who said it, and then says God sent Jesus (Acts 3:22-26). Stephen quotes it again in his defense (Acts 7:37). Acts reads 'The Lord God' where Deuteronomy reads 'The LORD your God', and does not carry 'from among you'. Acts 3:23 is not a word for word quotation of verse 19: Deuteronomy says God will require it of him, and Acts says that soul shall be destroyed from the people. Identifying the prophet as Jesus is Peter's own claim, running through the sermon to Acts 3:26.

The line from the end of the book is marked interpretive. Deuteronomy 34:10 says no prophet like Moses has arisen in Israel since, and many readers set that beside this promise and conclude that it was still waiting when the book closed. The verbal echo is real, 'like me' here and 'like Moses' there, but Deuteronomy does not draw the conclusion. Faithful readers differ on how much weight that last verse carries.

nt: This is the Deuteronomy verse the apostles quote most directly about Jesus. Peter quotes it in Acts 3:22-23 and Stephen in Acts 7:37. The Larger Catechism 42, on why our mediator was called Christ, prints Deuteronomy 18:18 and Acts 3:21-22 among its Scripture proofs, under the office of prophet.
questions: What had the people asked for that God is answering here?
What does God promise to put in the prophet's mouth?
Why might a reader want more than this verse before naming the prophet?

context: This is a law about what to do with a body. If a man has been executed for a capital crime and his body is hung on a tree, it is not to stay there overnight. He is to be buried the same day.
The reason given is that a hanged man is cursed by God, and that leaving him hanging would defile the land God is giving them.
The law is about burial and about the land. It is not about crucifixion. Paul is the one who brings this verse and the cross together.

passages.text: And if a man has committed a crime punishable by death and he is put to death, and you hang him on a tree,

his body shall not remain all night on the tree, but you shall bury him the same day, for a hanged man is cursed by God. You shall not defile your land that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance.

connections.text: Paul writes 'for it is written' and quotes this verse (Galatians 3:13), in the words 'Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree'. Deuteronomy reads 'a hanged man is cursed by God'. Paul says everyone, and he does not repeat the words by God. What he does with the verse is his own argument: he applies the curse Deuteronomy names to the death of Jesus on the cross. Deuteronomy is giving a burial law. Paul is explaining a crucifixion.

nt: Paul quotes this verse once, in Galatians 3:13, in the sentence about Christ redeeming us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us. The Shorter Catechism 27, on Christ's humiliation, names the cursed death of the cross, and Galatians 3:13 is among the Scripture proofs printed with that answer.
questions: What is this law regulating?
Why would Israel be told to bury such a body the same day?
What does Paul add when he quotes it, and what does he not change?

context: Near the end of the book Moses sets up a ceremony. The Levites read out a list of curses, and after each one the people answer Amen.
The last curse in the list is the widest. Cursed be anyone who does not confirm the words of this law by doing them. Not one law. The whole of it.
Chapter 28 then lays out blessings for obedience and curses for disobedience at length. Both lists start the same way. These will come upon you and overtake you.

passages.text: Cursed be anyone who does not confirm the words of this law by doing them.
And all these blessings shall come upon you and overtake you, if you obey the voice of the LORD your God.
But if you will not obey the voice of the LORD your God or be careful to do all his commandments and his statutes that I command you today, then all these curses shall come upon you and overtake you.

connections.text: Paul quotes this curse with the words 'for it is written' to show that anyone who relies on keeping the law is under it (Galatians 3:10). He gives it as 'Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the Book of the Law, and do them', where Deuteronomy reads 'Cursed be anyone who does not confirm the words of this law by doing them'. Everyone and all sharpen the point Deuteronomy is already making: all of it, not most of it.
Chapter 30 opens by pointing back to 'the blessing and the curse, which I have set before you'. That is this list. The text makes the link itself, and the turn that follows is the next stop.

nt: Paul uses this verse as the hinge of his argument in Galatians 3. If the law is the way in, then the law's own last curse shuts the door, because no one confirms all of it. Three verses later he says Christ took that curse. The curse list and the cross are joined by Paul, not by Deuteronomy.
questions: How wide is the last curse in the list?
What do the people say after each curse is read?
If the law's blessing depends on keeping all of it, where does that leave the reader?

context: After the curses, Moses turns. He says the commandment he has been giving is not too hard and not far off (30:11).
It is not in heaven, so that someone would have to go up and fetch it. It is not across the sea, so that someone would have to sail for it. It is near. In the mouth and in the heart.
Then he puts the choice in front of them. Life and good, death and evil. He calls heaven and earth as witnesses and tells them to choose life, so that they and their offspring may live (30:19).

passages.text: For this commandment that I command you today is not too hard for you, neither is it far off.
But the word is very near you. It is in your mouth and in your heart, so that you can do it.
I call heaven and earth to witness against you today, that I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse. Therefore choose life, that you and your offspring may live,

connections.text: Chapter 30 opens by naming the blessing and the curse that Moses had set before them, which is the list in chapters 27 and 28. The link is in the text.

Paul quotes verse 14 directly in Romans 10:8. He also reworks verses 12 and 13. Deuteronomy asks who will go up to heaven or over the sea to bring the commandment. Paul asks who will bring Christ down from heaven or up from the dead, and he puts the abyss where Deuteronomy has the sea. He changes the object of the question, from the commandment to Christ, and he does it deliberately. The quotation of verse 14 is word for word. The reworking of 12 and 13 is Paul's own reading.

Chapter 31 turns from the law to the song. God tells Moses to write the song and teach it (31:19), Moses writes it the same day (31:22), and he speaks it to the whole assembly (31:30). The sequence is in the narrative. It joins the law as a whole to the song, rather than this one passage in chapter 30 to the song.

nt: Paul takes this passage as the voice of the righteousness that comes by faith, and the word that is near becomes, in his hands, the message about Christ that is preached and believed. He adds the explanation himself: that is the word of faith that we proclaim (Romans 10:8). Deuteronomy was speaking about the commandment. Paul says the pattern holds for the gospel.
questions: What two places does Moses say the word is not?
Where does he say it is?
Paul applies this to the message about Christ. What does he keep from Moses, and what does he change?

context: Moses speaks a song in the hearing of the whole assembly of Israel (31:30). Chapter 32 is that song.

It opens by calling heaven and earth to listen, and it names God the Rock, whose work is perfect and whose ways are all justice. Then it turns to the people, and the news is not good. They have dealt corruptly with him. They are a crooked and twisted generation.
One line in the song matters for Paul. God says he will make them jealous with what is no people, and provoke them to anger with a foolish nation (32:21).

passages.text: Give ear, O heavens, and I will speak, and let the earth hear the words of my mouth.
The Rock, his work is perfect, for all his ways are justice.

They have made me jealous with what is no god; they have provoked me to anger with their idols. So I will make them jealous with those who are no people; I will provoke them to anger with a foolish nation.

connections.text: Chapter 31 turns from the law to the song. God tells Moses to write the song and teach it (31:19), Moses writes it the same day (31:22), and he speaks it to the whole assembly (31:30). The sequence is in the narrative. It joins the law as a whole to the song, rather than this one passage in chapter 30 to the song.

Paul writes 'First Moses says' and quotes verse 21 (Romans 10:19). The wording shifts from third person to second: Deuteronomy says God will make them jealous with those who are no people, and Paul says I will make you jealous of those who are not a nation. Naming Moses as the speaker is Paul's own, and it is a fair reading, since Deuteronomy 31:30 says Moses spoke the song.
Moses finishes reciting the song (32:44-45), blesses the tribes before his death (33:1), and dies in Moab (34:5). The book runs from the song to the death.

nt: Paul quotes verse 21 in Romans 10:19 to argue that Israel's unbelief and the welcome of the nations were both spoken of long before, in a song Israel was given to memorize. The song is a warning about what the people would become. Paul reads it as having come true.
questions: What does the song call God in verse 4?
Why would God give a song rather than only a speech?
What does Paul hear in verse 21 that he uses in his own argument?

context: Moses goes up Mount Nebo, and God shows him the land, from Gilead as far as Dan (34:1). He sees it. He does not enter it.

He dies there in the land of Moab, and the book calls him the servant of the LORD (34:5). Joshua takes his place, full of the spirit of wisdom, with Moses' hands having been laid on him, and the people obey him (34:9).
The last words about Moses are an assessment. No prophet like him has arisen in Israel since, whom the LORD knew face to face, with the signs and wonders he did in Egypt.

passages.text: Then Moses went up from the plains of Moab to Mount Nebo, to the top of Pisgah, which is opposite Jericho. And the LORD showed him all the land, Gilead as far as Dan,
So Moses the servant of the LORD died there in the land of Moab, according to the word of the LORD,
And there has not arisen a prophet since in Israel like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face

connections.text: The song ends, Moses blesses the tribes before his death, and then he dies. The book itself carries the reader from one to the other.

This is the one interpretive line on this map. Verse 10 says no prophet like Moses has arisen in Israel since. Many readers set that beside the promise in 18:15 and conclude that the promised prophet had not yet come when the book closed. The words do echo: 18:15 promises a prophet 'like me', and 34:10 says none 'like Moses' has arisen. The echo is in the text. The conclusion is not. Some readers hear verse 10 as a note on the prophets up to the writer's own day instead of a statement about the future, so the map draws this line dashed.

nt: The New Testament does not quote Deuteronomy 34. The verse the apostles quote is the promise four stops back, in chapter 18. What this chapter adds, for readers who hear it that way, is that the promise was still open when the book of Moses ended.
questions: What does Moses see, and what does he not get to do?
What does the book say about him in its last lines?
Does verse 10 look back only, or does it leave something open? Give your reason.

context: After his baptism Jesus is led by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tested by the devil (Matthew 4:1). He fasts forty days and nights, and he is hungry (4:2).

Three tests come. Make bread out of these stones. Throw yourself from the temple. Take all the kingdoms of the world. Jesus answers each one with a sentence from Deuteronomy, and each time he says it is written.
Luke tells the same three tests but puts the kingdoms before the temple (Luke 4:5-12). The three answers are the same three verses.

passages.text: Then Jesus was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil.
Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God.
Jesus said to him, “Again it is written, ‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.’”

connections.text: The first answer quotes Deuteronomy 8:3, the verse about not living by bread alone. Matthew reads 'the mouth of God' where Deuteronomy reads 'the mouth of the LORD'.

The second and third answers both come from Deuteronomy 6. Matthew 4:7 quotes 6:16 almost word for word. Matthew 4:10 reads 'You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve' where 6:13 reads 'It is the LORD your God you shall fear. Him you shall serve'. Both answers are introduced with it is written.

nt: All three answers come from one short stretch of Deuteronomy, chapters 6 and 8. Jesus does not debate the devil about the law. He quotes it. The wording of each answer differs a little from the ESV of Deuteronomy, because the New Testament writers generally quote the Old Testament in Greek. Matthew 4:4 reads 'the mouth of God' for 'the mouth of the LORD'. Matthew 4:10 reads 'worship' for 'fear' and adds the word only. Matthew 4:7 matches almost word for word.
questions: What is Jesus' physical condition when the first test comes?
Where do all three of his answers come from?
Why does it matter that he answers with Scripture rather than with power?

context: The Pharisees have heard that Jesus silenced the Sadducees. One of them, a lawyer, asks a question to test him. Which is the great commandment in the Law (Matthew 22:34-36)?
Jesus answers with Deuteronomy 6:5. Love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your mind. He calls it the great and first commandment.
Then he adds a second, that you shall love your neighbor as yourself, and says that all the Law and the Prophets depend on the two of them.

passages.text: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind.
This is the great and first commandment.
On these two commandments depend all the Law and the Prophets.

connections.text: Jesus is quoting Deuteronomy 6:5 and saying it is first. Matthew reads 'with all your mind' where Deuteronomy reads 'with all your might'. Mark 12:30 has four terms, heart, soul, mind, and strength, and Mark also keeps the line before it about the Lord being one. Matthew marks the quotation with no formula. He gives the words as Jesus' answer, and the source is not in dispute.

nt: Mark's account is worth reading beside Matthew's. Mark keeps Deuteronomy 6:4 in front of the command, so Jesus says that God is one and then says to love him (Mark 12:29-30). Matthew starts at the command. Matthew has three terms and Mark has four, and neither Gospel comments on the difference. Between them they quote the Shema the way Deuteronomy has it, with the statement about God first and the command second.
questions: What question was Jesus asked, and why was it asked?
Which commandment does he put first, and where is it from?
What does he mean that all the Law and the Prophets depend on these two?

context: A man who could not walk has been healed at the temple gate and a crowd has gathered. Peter preaches to them. He tells them they acted in ignorance, and that what God foretold through all the prophets, that his Christ would suffer, has been fulfilled (Acts 3:17-18).

Then he quotes Moses. The Lord God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers, and you shall listen to him in whatever he tells you (3:22). The next sentence restates rather than quotes Deuteronomy 18:19: every soul who does not listen to that prophet shall be destroyed from the people (3:23).

Peter does not leave the identification open. He ends by saying that God raised up his servant and sent him to bless them by turning them from their wickedness (3:26). Stephen quotes the same promise later, in his own defense (Acts 7:37).

passages.text: Moses said, ‘The Lord God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers. You shall listen to him in whatever he tells you.
And it shall be that every soul who does not listen to that prophet shall be destroyed from the people.’
This is the Moses who said to the Israelites, ‘God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers.’

connections.text: Peter names Moses as the speaker and quotes Deuteronomy 18:15-19. Acts reads 'The Lord God' where Deuteronomy reads 'The LORD your God', and does not carry 'from among you'. Acts 3:23 restates verse 19 rather than quoting it: Deuteronomy says God will require it of him, and Acts says that soul shall be destroyed from the people. Identifying that prophet as Jesus is Peter's own claim, which the sermon makes as it closes.

nt: Acts quotes the promise in a shorter form than Deuteronomy gives it, and Stephen's version is shorter still. The apostles are quoting a verse their hearers already knew, and the point they add is the identification. The Larger Catechism 42 prints Deuteronomy 18:18 and Acts 3:21-22 together among its Scripture proofs, under Christ holding the office of prophet.
questions: What had just happened that drew the crowd?
What does Peter say the prophets had foretold?
Where exactly does Peter say that the prophet is Jesus?

context: Paul is writing to Christians in Galatia who were being told that they had to keep the law in order to belong to God's people. His answer runs through Abraham, the law, and the promise.
He says that everyone who relies on works of the law is under a curse, and he quotes the last curse of Deuteronomy 27 to prove it (3:10). The law offers no credit for keeping most of it.

Then comes the turn. Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, and to say it Paul quotes Deuteronomy 21:23 about the hanged man (3:13). The blessing promised to Abraham reaches the nations through that (3:14).

passages.text: For all who rely on works of the law are under a curse; for it is written, “Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the Book of the Law, and do them.”
Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us
for it is written, “Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree”
so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles, so that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith.

connections.text: Paul quotes Deuteronomy 27:26 with the words 'for it is written'. He gives it as 'Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the Book of the Law, and do them'. Deuteronomy reads 'Cursed be anyone who does not confirm the words of this law by doing them'.

Paul quotes Deuteronomy 21:23, again with 'for it is written', as 'Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree'. Deuteronomy reads 'a hanged man is cursed by God'. Deuteronomy is giving a law about burying an executed man the same day. Applying the curse to the cross is Paul's argument.

nt: Paul takes two laws that stand far apart in Deuteronomy and sets them together. One is the curse on anyone who fails to keep the whole law. The other is a burial rule that calls a hanged man cursed. Deuteronomy never joins them. Paul joins them at the cross, and that joining is the heart of his case. The Shorter Catechism 27 names the cursed death of the cross in its answer on Christ's humiliation, and Galatians 3:13 is among the Scripture proofs printed with it.
questions: What does Paul say about anyone who relies on works of the law?
Which two verses from Deuteronomy does he quote, and what is each one about in its own place?
What does he say Christ did with the curse?

context: Paul is writing about his own people and their unbelief. He sets two kinds of righteousness beside each other. One is based on the law, where the person who does the commandments shall live by them (10:5). The other is based on faith.

For the second he reaches for Deuteronomy 30. Do not say, who will ascend into heaven, which Paul reads as bringing Christ down. Do not say, who will descend into the abyss, which he reads as bringing Christ up from the dead (10:6-7).

Then the quotation itself. The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart. Paul adds what he takes it to mean: that is the word of faith that we proclaim (10:8). Confess with the mouth, believe in the heart (10:9).

passages.text: For Moses writes about the righteousness that is based on the law, that the person who does the commandments shall live by them.
The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart
because, if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.

connections.text: Verse 8 quotes Deuteronomy 30:14 word for word. Verses 6 and 7 rework Deuteronomy 30:12-13, changing the object of the questions from the commandment to Christ, and putting the abyss where Deuteronomy has the sea. Paul makes those changes openly and they are visible in the words.
Later in the same chapter Paul writes 'First Moses says' and quotes the Song of Moses, Deuteronomy 32:21 (Romans 10:19). Deuteronomy has God making them jealous; Paul has him making you jealous.

nt: Romans 10 uses Deuteronomy twice, and in two different ways. The word that is near becomes the preached message about Christ, and the song's warning about a foolish nation becomes an argument that Israel's unbelief was spoken of long before. The Shorter Catechism 86 defines faith in Jesus Christ as receiving and resting upon him alone for salvation, as he is offered in the gospel, which is the doctrine this passage is usually read to teach. Romans 10 is not among the proofs printed with that answer.

What does Paul say the near word is?
Where does the mouth and the heart turn up again a verse later?

context: Isaiah 1:1 works like a title page. It names the prophet, his father Amoz, and the four kings of Judah he served under: Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. That covers roughly the second half of the 700s BC.

The first chapter reads like a court case. God calls heaven and earth as witnesses and says the children he raised have rebelled against him (1:2). The people are busy with sacrifices and feasts, and God says he is weary of them, because their hands are full of blood (1:11-15). What he asks for is plain: stop doing evil, learn to do good, seek justice (1:16-17).
Then comes the invitation. God offers to reason with them, and he promises that scarlet sins can be made white as snow. The chapter does not yet say how. The rest of the book does.

passages.text: The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master's crib, but Israel does not know, my people do not understand.
Come now, let us reason together, says the LORD: though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they are red like crimson, they shall become like wool.

connections.text: The link is a king's name. Isaiah 1:1 lists Uzziah first among the kings Isaiah served under, and Isaiah 6:1 dates the vision of the throne to the year Uzziah died. The book does not say whether chapters 1 to 5 were preached before or after that vision, and readers differ on it.

nt: Paul quotes Isaiah 1:9 in Romans 9:29, naming Isaiah: if the Lord had not left offspring, his people would have been like Sodom. This stop has no line to a New Testament stop on this map.

What does God ask the people to do instead?
What does he promise about sins that are like scarlet?

context: King Uzziah had reigned for about fifty years. In the year he died, Isaiah saw the true King. The Lord sits on a throne, and the train of his robe fills the temple. Seraphim call to one another that he is holy, holy, holy.

Isaiah's first word is woe. He is a man of unclean lips among a people of unclean lips, and he has seen the King (6:5). One of the seraphim touches his mouth with a burning coal from the altar and says his guilt is taken away and his sin atoned for (6:7). Only then does Isaiah hear the question, Whom shall I send?

The mission is hard. He is to preach to people whose hearts will grow dull as they hear him (6:9-10). When he asks how long, the answer is until the land is laid waste. Yet the chapter ends with a stump left standing, and it calls the holy seed its stump (6:13).

passages.text: In the year that King Uzziah died I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up; and the train of his robe filled the temple.
And I said: “Woe is me! For I am lost; for I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips; for my eyes have seen the King, the LORD of hosts!”
And I heard the voice of the Lord saying, “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” Then I said, “Here I am! Send me.”

connections.text: The link is a king's name. Isaiah 1:1 lists Uzziah first among the kings Isaiah served under, and Isaiah 6:1 dates the vision of the throne to the year Uzziah died. The book does not say whether chapters 1 to 5 were preached before or after that vision, and readers differ on it.

The book moves from one king to the next. Chapter 6 is dated to the death of Uzziah. Chapter 7 opens in the days of Ahaz and names him as the son of Jotham, son of Uzziah. Isaiah was told in chapter 6 that the people would not listen. In chapter 7 a king does not listen.

John writes 'For again Isaiah said' and quotes Isaiah 6:10 (John 12:39-40). The wording differs. In Isaiah it is a command to the prophet: 'Make the heart of this people dull, and their ears heavy, and blind their eyes'. In John it is a statement: 'He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart'. John leaves out the ears. Then John says Isaiah said these things because he saw his glory and spoke of him (12:41). In John's telling, the glory Isaiah saw in the temple was the glory of Christ. That claim is John's own, and he makes it openly.

nt: Isaiah 6:9-10 is one of the Old Testament passages the New Testament quotes most often. Jesus quotes it to explain why he teaches in parables (Matthew 13:14-15). Paul quotes it to the Jewish leaders in Rome (Acts 28:25-27). John quotes it in John 12:40 and adds that Isaiah saw Christ's glory. In Revelation 4:8 the living creatures around the throne sing holy, holy, holy, as the seraphim do here.
questions: What does Isaiah say about himself when he sees the Lord?
What has to happen before he is sent?
What is he told about how people will respond to his preaching?

context: The year is about 735 BC. The kings of Syria and of northern Israel have joined forces against Judah, and the heart of King Ahaz shakes like trees in the wind (7:2). Isaiah meets him by the water supply and tells him not to fear. These two kings are smoldering stumps of firebrands.

God offers Ahaz a sign, as deep as Sheol or as high as heaven. Ahaz answers that he will not put the LORD to the test. It sounds devout, but 2 Kings 16:7-9 shows he had another plan, which was to pay Assyria for protection. So the Lord himself gives a sign: the virgin will conceive and bear a son, and call his name Immanuel.

Isaiah ties the sign to the near future. Before the boy knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good, the land of the two kings Ahaz dreads will be deserted (7:16). Readers differ on whether a child born in Isaiah's day was a first stage of the sign. Matthew says plainly that the birth of Jesus fulfilled it.

passages.text: If you are not firm in faith, you will not be firm at all.
Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.

connections.text: The book moves from one king to the next. Chapter 6 is dated to the death of Uzziah. Chapter 7 opens in the days of Ahaz and names him as the son of Jotham, son of Uzziah. Isaiah was told in chapter 6 that the people would not listen. In chapter 7 a king does not listen.

Chapters 7 to 9 are one stretch of the book, set in the same crisis. The name Immanuel comes back in Isaiah 8:8, and 8:10 says God is with us. Chapter 8 ends in gloom and darkness, and 9:1-2 answers with a great light. That much is in the text. Isaiah does not say in so many words that the child of 9:6 is the son called Immanuel in 7:14. Christian readers put them together, with good reason, but that step is a reading and not a quotation.

The two scenes happen at the same spot. Isaiah meets Ahaz 'at the end of the conduit of the upper pool on the highway to the Washer's Field' (7:3). A generation later the Assyrian officer stands 'by the conduit of the upper pool on the highway to the Washer's Field' (36:2). The place is named in both. Many readers think the book wants the two kings compared, Ahaz who would not trust and Hezekiah who prayed. The comparison is a reading. The shared place is in the text.

Matthew writes that all this took place to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet, and then quotes Isaiah 7:14 (Matthew 1:22-23). The citation is explicit. Matthew reads 'they shall call his name Immanuel' where Isaiah reads 'shall call his name Immanuel', and Matthew adds the meaning of the name. In Isaiah 7 the sign is tied to a near event: before the boy knows how to refuse evil and choose good, the two kings Ahaz fears will be gone (7:16). Readers differ on whether a child in Isaiah's own day was a first stage of the sign. Matthew's claim about Jesus is plain either way.

nt: Matthew 1:22-23 quotes Isaiah 7:14 and says the virgin birth of Jesus took place to fulfill it. Matthew also translates the name: God with us.
questions: What is Ahaz afraid of, and what does Isaiah tell him?
Why does Ahaz refuse the sign, and what does God do then?
What does the name Immanuel mean, and who tells you?

context: Chapter 8 ends in distress and thick darkness. Chapter 9 begins with but. The lands of Zebulun and Naphtali, in Galilee, were the first to be overrun by Assyria (2 Kings 15:29). Isaiah says those same lands will be made glorious, and the people who walked in darkness will see a great light.

The joy has a cause. The yoke is broken, the boots of war are burned, and a child is born. He carries the government on his shoulder. He has four names, and two of them, Mighty God and Everlasting Father, are more than any ordinary king could bear.
He reigns on the throne of David with justice and righteousness, from this time forth and forevermore. Isaiah adds who will make sure of it: the zeal of the LORD of hosts will do this (9:7).

passages.text: The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light; those who dwelt in a land of deep darkness, on them has light shone.
For to us a child is born, to us a son is given; and the government shall be upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace.

Chapter 8 ends in gloom and darkness, and 9:1-2 answers with a great light. That much is in the text. Isaiah does not say in so many words that the child of 9:6 is the son called Immanuel in 7:14. This line is marked interpretive. Isaiah 9:7 puts the child on the throne of David. Isaiah 11:1 speaks of a shoot from the stump of Jesse, and Jesse was David's father. Both passages describe a just and lasting rule from David's family, and most readers take them as one king. Isaiah does not say so himself. The New Testament applies Isaiah 11:10 to Jesus (Romans 15:12) and gives him the throne of David (Luke 1:32-33).

Matthew names the prophet Isaiah and quotes Isaiah 9:1-2 (Matthew 4:14-16). The wording shifts a little. Isaiah has 'The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light'. Matthew has 'the people dwelling in darkness have seen a great light'. Matthew quotes the light in Galilee. He does not quote the child of Isaiah 9:6-7. Christians read those verses of Jesus because of the quotation Matthew does make and because Gabriel promises Mary's son the throne of David (Luke 1:32-33).

nt: Matthew 4:14-16 quotes Isaiah 9:1-2 when Jesus settles in Capernaum. No New Testament writer quotes Isaiah 9:6-7 directly. Gabriel's words to Mary come close to its themes: her son will be given the throne of his father David, and of his kingdom there will be no end (Luke 1:32-33).
questions: Which part of the land sees the light first, and why does that matter?
What four names is the child given?
Who does Isaiah say will bring this about?

context: Chapter 10 ends with the LORD cutting down a proud forest. Chapter 11 begins with one small shoot. The royal house of David will be brought so low that Isaiah calls it a stump, and he names it after Jesse, David's father, as if the family had gone back to its humble start.

The shoot is a king. The Spirit of the LORD rests on him with wisdom, understanding, counsel, might, knowledge, and the fear of the LORD. He does not judge by what his eyes see. He decides with equity for the meek of the earth.

His rule changes the world. The wolf dwells with the lamb, a little child leads them, and the earth is full of the knowledge of the LORD as the waters cover the sea. In that day the root of Jesse stands as a signal for the peoples, and the nations inquire of him (11:10).

passages.text: There shall come forth a shoot from the stump of Jesse, and a branch from his roots shall bear fruit.
And the Spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and might, the Spirit of knowledge and the fear of the LORD.
