The New Testament applies Isaiah 11:10 to Jesus (Romans 15:12) and gives him the throne of David (Luke 1:32-33).

nt: Paul quotes Isaiah 11:10 in Romans 15:12, naming Isaiah, as proof that the Gentiles would hope in Christ. In Revelation Jesus is called the Root of David (Revelation 5:5, 22:16). This map has no New Testament stop for those texts, so the stop's only line is the interpretive one from the child of chapter 9.
questions: Why does Isaiah speak of a stump?
What rests on this king, and how does he judge?
Who comes looking for the root of Jesse in verse 10?

context: Chapters 13 to 23 are a run of messages about the nations. Babylon comes first. Isaiah 13 describes the day of the LORD falling on the city, and says God is stirring up the Medes against it (13:17). Babylon, the glory of kingdoms, will become a ruin where wild animals live.

Chapter 14 gives Israel a taunt to take up against the king of Babylon once God has given them rest. The king who said in his heart that he would ascend to heaven is brought down to Sheol. Isaiah 21:9 adds the short cry that Revelation repeats: fallen, fallen is Babylon.

Interpretation: Isaiah 14:12, 'How you are fallen from heaven, O Day Star, son of Dawn', is spoken to the king of Babylon (14:4). Some Christians have also read it as a picture of the fall of Satan. The passage itself does not say that, and many Reformed readers, John Calvin among them, take it of the king alone.

passages.text: And Babylon, the glory of kingdoms, the splendor and pomp of the Chaldeans, will be like Sodom and Gomorrah when God overthrew them.
you will take up this taunt against the king of Babylon: “How the oppressor has ceased, the insolent fury ceased!
Fallen, fallen is Babylon; and all the carved images of her gods he has shattered to the ground.

nt: Revelation 14:8 and 18:2 take up the cry 'Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great'. Revelation does not cite Isaiah by name. No line on this map reaches this stop, because none of the New Testament stops here quotes these chapters. The Revelation map has the fall of Babylon as a stop of its own.
questions: What did the king of Babylon say in his heart, and where does he end up?
Why would God's people need a song like this before Babylon had even risen?
What does this passage say about every proud power?

context: It is 701 BC, the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah. Sennacherib of Assyria has taken the fortified towns of Judah. His officer, the Rabshakeh, stands outside Jerusalem and shouts in Hebrew so that everyone on the wall can hear. No god of any nation has saved his land from Assyria, he says. Why would the LORD save Jerusalem?

Hezekiah tears his clothes and sends to Isaiah. When a letter comes repeating the threat, he takes it into the house of the LORD and spreads it out before him. His prayer asks God to save for the sake of his own name.

Isaiah sends the answer. The king of Assyria will not shoot an arrow there. The angel of the LORD strikes down 185,000 in the Assyrian camp (37:36). Sennacherib goes back to Nineveh, where his own sons later kill him. Sennacherib's own record of the campaign survives. It lists the towns he took and says he shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem like a bird in a cage. It does not claim he took the city.

passages.text: Hezekiah received the letter from the hand of the messengers, and read it; and Hezekiah went up to the house of the LORD, and spread it before the LORD.
So now, O LORD our God, save us from his hand, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you alone are the LORD.

connections.text: The two scenes happen at the same spot. Isaiah meets Ahaz 'at the end of the conduit of the upper pool on the highway to the Washer's Field' (7:3). A generation later the Assyrian officer stands 'by the conduit of the upper pool on the highway to the Washer's Field' (36:2). The place is named in both. Many readers think the book wants the two kings compared, Ahaz who would not trust and Hezekiah who prayed. The comparison is a reading. The shared place is in the text.

This is the order of the book. The Hezekiah chapters end with Isaiah telling the king that everything in his house will be carried to Babylon (39:5-7). The very next words are 'Comfort, comfort my people' (40:1), spoken to a Jerusalem whose warfare is ended and whose iniquity is pardoned (40:2). Isaiah sets the warning and the comfort side by side. He does not add a sentence that joins them.

nt: The New Testament does not quote these chapters. The same story is told in 2 Kings 18 to 19 and 2 Chronicles 32.
questions: What argument does the Assyrian officer use against trusting the LORD?
What does Hezekiah do with the letter?
What reason does he give God for saving the city?

context: From chapter 40 on, the book speaks to people who need comfort. Chapter 39 has just warned that Judah's treasures and sons will be carried to Babylon. Now God says comfort twice, and tells the speaker to say that Jerusalem's warfare is ended and her iniquity pardoned.

A voice cries out to prepare the way of the LORD in the wilderness. Valleys are to be lifted and mountains made low, because the glory of the LORD will be revealed and all flesh will see it together. Another voice says that people are like grass, but the word of our God will stand forever.
The good news to be shouted from a high mountain is short: behold your God. He comes with might, and he tends his flock like a shepherd and carries the lambs in his arms (40:9-11).

passages.text: Comfort, comfort my people, says your God.
The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever.
He will tend his flock like a shepherd; he will gather the lambs in his arms; he will carry them in his bosom, and gently lead those that are with young.

The very next words are 'Comfort, comfort my people' (40:1), spoken to a Jerusalem whose warfare is ended and whose iniquity is pardoned (40:2). Isaiah sets the warning and the comfort side by side. He does not add a sentence that joins them.

Chapter 40 sends comfort to Jerusalem and the cities of Judah. Isaiah 44:26-28 says how the comfort will come: God says of Jerusalem that she shall be inhabited, of the cities of Judah that they shall be built, and of Cyrus that he is God's shepherd. The same cities are named in both places.

nt: All four Gospels quote Isaiah 40:3 about John the Baptist (Matthew 3:3, Mark 1:3, Luke 3:4-6, John 1:23). The road is made ready for the LORD, and the one who comes down it is Jesus. Peter quotes Isaiah 40:6-8 and says this word is the good news that was preached to you (1 Peter 1:24-25). This map has no stop for those texts.
questions: What is Jerusalem to be told in verse 2?
Who is the road being prepared for?
What lasts when people fade like grass?

context: God says behold, and presents his servant. He upholds him, delights in him, and has put his Spirit on him. The servant's task is very large: to bring forth justice to the nations.

His manner is the surprise. He will not cry aloud or lift up his voice in the street. A bruised reed he will not break, and a faintly burning wick he will not quench. He himself will not grow faint until justice is established on the earth (42:4).

God then speaks to the servant directly. He will give him as a covenant for the people and a light for the nations, to open blind eyes and bring prisoners out of the dungeon (42:6-7). Elsewhere in these chapters the nation Israel is called God's servant (41:8). Here the servant does for Israel and the nations what Israel could not do.

passages.text: Behold my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights; I have put my Spirit upon him; he will bring forth justice to the nations.
a bruised reed he will not break, and a faintly burning wick he will not quench; he will faithfully bring forth justice.

connections.text: This line is marked interpretive. Both passages speak of God's servant and of a light for the nations (42:6 and 49:6). Reading them as two songs about one person is a very old and very common reading, but the grouping called the Servant Songs comes from later readers and not from Isaiah. Isaiah also calls the nation Israel God's servant (41:8), and 49:3 addresses the servant as Israel, while 49:5-6 gives him a mission to Israel. Readers work that out in different ways.

nt: Matthew 12:17-21 quotes Isaiah 42:1-4 at length and says Jesus' quiet healing ministry fulfilled it. Many readers also hear this verse in the Father's words at Jesus' baptism, 'with whom I am well pleased' (Matthew 3:17). That second link is an echo that readers notice, not a marked quotation.
questions: What has God put on his servant?
How does the servant treat the weak?
How far does his work reach?

context: In these chapters God argues against the idols. They cannot say what is coming. He can, and he gives a name: Cyrus. God calls him my shepherd, who will fulfill his purpose by saying that Jerusalem shall be built and the temple's foundation laid.

God even calls Cyrus his anointed (45:1). The word is the one from which we get messiah, and here it means a ruler God has appointed for a task. Cyrus is no worshiper of the LORD. God says twice, 'though you do not know me' (45:4-5). He does it for the sake of his servant Jacob, and so that people from east to west may know there is no other God.

Cyrus the Great of Persia took Babylon in 539 BC and let the exiles of Judah return (Ezra 1:1-4). Christians who hold that Isaiah wrote the whole book take this as a prophecy given about 150 years ahead, which is the very point God is making against the idols. Many modern scholars date these chapters to the time of Cyrus instead. The timeline gives both views.

passages.text: who says of Cyrus, ‘He is my shepherd, and he shall fulfill all my purpose’; saying of Jerusalem, ‘She shall be built,’ and of the temple, ‘Your foundation shall be laid.’”
For the sake of my servant Jacob, and Israel my chosen, I call you by your name, I name you, though you do not know me.

connections.text: Chapter 40 sends comfort to Jerusalem and the cities of Judah. Isaiah 44:26-28 says how the comfort will come: God says of Jerusalem that she shall be inhabited, of the cities of Judah that they shall be built, and of Cyrus that he is God's shepherd. The same cities are named in both places.

nt: The New Testament does not quote the Cyrus passage. Ezra 1:1-4 and 2 Chronicles 36:22-23 record his decree.
questions: What two titles does God give Cyrus?
Does Cyrus know the LORD? What does that show about how God rules?
Why does God name what will happen ahead of time?

context: The servant calls the coastlands and distant peoples to listen. The LORD called him from the womb and made his mouth like a sharp sword. God says to him, 'You are my servant, Israel, in whom I will be glorified' (49:3).
Then the servant admits discouragement. He has labored in vain and spent his strength for nothing. Yet he leaves his case with the LORD.

God's answer widens the mission. Bringing back the tribes of Jacob is too light a thing. The servant will be a light for the nations, so that salvation reaches the end of the earth. He is called Israel in verse 3, and he is sent to restore Israel in verses 5 and 6. So he bears the nation's name and does what the nation needs done for it.

passages.text: But I said, “I have labored in vain; I have spent my strength for nothing and vanity; yet surely my right is with the LORD, and my recompense with my God.”
I will make you as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth.

Reading them as two songs about one person is a very old and very common reading, but the grouping called the Servant Songs comes from later readers and not from Isaiah. Isaiah also calls the nation Israel God's servant (41:8), and 49:3 addresses the servant as Israel, while 49:5-6 gives him a mission to Israel. Readers work that out in different ways.

This line is marked interpretive. In chapter 49 the servant says he has labored in vain. In chapter 50 a speaker tells of being struck and spat on, and 50:10 calls him the LORD's servant. Most readers hear the same voice in both. Isaiah does not label them as a series.

nt: Paul and Barnabas quote Isaiah 49:6 in Acts 13:47 as the Lord's command to them when they turn to the Gentiles. The servant's mission is carried on through Christ's messengers. Simeon calls the child Jesus 'a light for revelation to the Gentiles' (Luke 2:32), words close to this verse. This map has no stop for those texts.

What does God call too light a thing?
Who is the light for?

context: The speaker has the tongue of those who are taught, so that he can sustain the weary with a word. Morning by morning the Lord GOD wakens his ear. Unlike Israel, he says he was not rebellious and did not turn backward.
Obedience costs him. He gives his back to those who strike and his cheeks to those who pull out the beard. He does not hide his face from disgrace and spitting.

He is not crushed by it. The Lord GOD helps him, so he sets his face like a flint and knows he will not be put to shame. He who vindicates him is near. Verse 10 then asks who among the hearers fears the LORD and obeys the voice of his servant.

passages.text: I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard; I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting.
But the Lord GOD helps me; therefore I have not been disgraced; therefore I have set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be put to shame.

This line is marked interpretive. The servant who gives his back to those who strike (50:6) is read as the same servant whose appearance is marred (52:14) and who does not open his mouth (53:7). The suffering grows from one passage to the next. The link between them is the word servant and the likeness of what is described. It is a reading, and a widely shared one.

nt: No New Testament writer quotes this passage with a citation. The Gospels record that Jesus was struck, scourged, and spat on (Matthew 26:67, 27:26-30), and Luke says he set his face to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51). Christians have long read those scenes beside this passage. That is a likeness readers see, and the Gospels do not point it out themselves.
questions: What does the servant do every morning?
What does he suffer, and does he resist?
Why is he sure he will not be put to shame?

context: The passage begins with God speaking: my servant shall be high and lifted up. Then it shows the road to that height. His appearance is marred. He grows up like a root out of dry ground, with no beauty that we should desire him. He is despised and rejected, a man of sorrows.

The center of the chapter explains why he suffers. The griefs he carries are ours. He is pierced for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities, and the LORD lays on him the iniquity of us all. He is silent like a lamb led to the slaughter. He is cut off out of the land of the living and given a grave.

And then he lives. It was the will of the LORD to crush him, and when his soul makes an offering for guilt, he shall see his offspring and prolong his days (53:10). By his knowledge the righteous one, God's servant, makes many to be accounted righteous, and he bears their iniquities (53:11).

passages.text: He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief; and as one from whom men hide their faces he was despised, and we esteemed him not.
But he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed.
He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth; like a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and like a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth.

The servant who gives his back to those who strike (50:6) is read as the same servant whose appearance is marred (52:14) and who does not open his mouth (53:7). John says the unbelief of the crowd happened so that the word spoken by the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled, and he quotes Isaiah 53:1 (John 12:38). John's quotation begins with the word 'Lord', which is not in the ESV of Isaiah 53:1. Otherwise the two match closely.

Luke gives the passage the Ethiopian was reading, and it is Isaiah 53:7-8 (Acts 8:32-33). The wording differs from the ESV of Isaiah. Acts has 'Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter and like a lamb before its shearer is silent', where Isaiah has the lamb led to the slaughter and the sheep silent before its shearers. Acts has 'In his humiliation justice was denied him', where Isaiah has 'By oppression and judgment he was taken away'. The man asks who the prophet is speaking about. Philip begins with this Scripture and tells him the good news about Jesus (8:35). The identification is Philip's, and Luke records it as the answer.

Peter uses the words of Isaiah 53 without any phrase such as it is written. The source is not in doubt. 1 Peter 2:22 reads 'He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth', where Isaiah 53:9 reads 'although he had done no violence, and there was no deceit in his mouth'. 1 Peter 2:24 reads 'By his wounds you have been healed', where Isaiah 53:5 reads 'with his wounds we are healed'. 1 Peter 2:25 says you were straying like sheep, and Isaiah 53:6 says all we like sheep have gone astray. Peter changes we to you because he is speaking to his readers.

nt: The New Testament quotes this passage many times. Matthew 8:17 quotes 53:4 about Jesus' healings. Jesus quotes 53:12 about himself on the night of his arrest: 'And he was numbered with the transgressors' (Luke 22:37). John 12:38 and Romans 10:16 quote 53:1. Acts 8:32-33 quotes 53:7-8. Peter draws on verses 4, 5, 6, and 9 in 1 Peter 2:22-25. Three of those texts are stops on this map.
questions: Whose sins does the servant suffer for?
How does he behave while he suffers?
What happens after his death in verses 10 to 12?

context: After the servant's work comes an open invitation. Everyone who thirsts is called to the waters. The one with no money is told to buy wine and milk without money and without price. God asks why people spend their wages on what does not satisfy.

He promises an everlasting covenant, 'my steadfast, sure love for David' (55:3). The offer has a time on it: seek the LORD while he may be found. The wicked are to forsake their way and return, because God will abundantly pardon. His thoughts are higher than ours, as the heavens are higher than the earth.
The chapter closes with a promise about God's word. Like rain that waters the earth and does not return without making it sprout, his word will accomplish what he purposes.

passages.text: Come, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters; and he who has no money, come, buy and eat! Come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.
let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts; let him return to the LORD, that he may have compassion on him, and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon.
so shall my word be that goes out from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish that which I purpose, and shall succeed in the thing for which I sent it.

nt: Paul quotes Isaiah 55:3 in Acts 13:34 and applies the sure blessings of David to the resurrection of Jesus. The invitation itself sounds again in John 7:37, where Jesus says that anyone who thirsts should come to him and drink, and in Revelation 22:17, where the one who is thirsty may take the water of life without price. Those two are echoes of the wording, not marked quotations. This map has no stop for these texts.
questions: What does the invitation cost the one who comes?
What does God promise the wicked person who returns?
What does God say about his own word?

context: Someone speaks in the first person. The Spirit of the Lord GOD is on him, because the LORD has anointed him. He is sent with a message, and the message is for the poor, the brokenhearted, the captives, and those who are bound.

He proclaims the year of the LORD's favor and the day of vengeance of our God, and he comforts all who mourn. The language of liberty recalls the year of jubilee in Leviticus 25:10, when debts were released and people went home.

Isaiah does not name the speaker. Earlier the Spirit rests on the shoot from Jesse (11:2) and on the servant (42:1), and many readers hear the same figure here. Jesus settled the question for his hearers in Nazareth by reading the passage and saying it was fulfilled that day.

passages.text: The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me, because the LORD has anointed me to bring good news to the poor; he has sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to those who are bound;
to proclaim the year of the LORD's favor, and the day of vengeance of our God; to comfort all who mourn;

connections.text: Luke says Jesus was given the scroll of the prophet Isaiah and found the place where this was written, and Jesus then says, 'Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing' (Luke 4:17-21). The citation is explicit. The wording in Luke is not identical to the ESV of Isaiah 61. Luke does not have 'to bind up the brokenhearted'. Luke has 'recovering of sight to the blind' where Isaiah has 'the opening of the prison to those who are bound'. Luke also has 'to set at liberty those who are oppressed', which is close to a line in Isaiah 58:6. And the reading stops at 'the year of the Lord's favor', before Isaiah's next words, 'the day of vengeance of our God'. Many readers think Jesus stopped there on purpose. Luke does not say why.

nt: Luke 4:16-21 is the direct use of this passage. Jesus also answers John the Baptist's question with words that recall it: the poor have good news preached to them (Luke 7:22).
questions: Who is the good news for?
What two things does the speaker proclaim in verse 2?
Which of the two did Jesus read aloud in Nazareth, and where did he stop?

context: The book that began by calling heaven and earth as witnesses ends with new heavens and a new earth. God creates them, and he creates Jerusalem to be a joy. The sound of weeping is heard no more.

Isaiah paints the new world in pictures his hearers knew: long life, houses lived in by those who built them, vineyards enjoyed by those who planted them. The wolf and the lamb graze together, which repeats the peace of chapter 11. They shall not hurt or destroy in all God's holy mountain.

The last chapter says the new heavens and new earth will remain, and all flesh will come to worship before the LORD. Its final verse is a hard one. It shows the end of those who rebelled against him (66:24). Isaiah does not let the reader forget that there are two ends.

passages.text: For behold, I create new heavens and a new earth, and the former things shall not be remembered or come into mind.
The wolf and the lamb shall graze together; the lion shall eat straw like the ox, and dust shall be the serpent's food. They shall not hurt or destroy in all my holy mountain,” says the LORD.

connections.text: This is shared wording and not a marked quotation. Revelation never introduces an Old Testament text with a phrase such as it is written. John sees 'a new heaven and a new earth' (Revelation 21:1), and Isaiah 65:17 promises 'new heavens and a new earth'. Revelation 21:4 says the former things have passed away, and Isaiah 65:17 says the former things shall not be remembered. Isaiah 65:19 promises an end to the sound of weeping, and Revelation 21:4 says God will wipe away every tear. 2 Peter 3:13 says Christians are waiting for new heavens and a new earth according to his promise, which points back to a promise like this one.

nt: 2 Peter 3:13 says we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth according to his promise. Revelation 21:1-5 shows them. Jesus uses the words of Isaiah 66:24 when he warns about hell (Mark 9:48). Interpretation: Isaiah 65:20 speaks of people dying at a great age, while Revelation 21:4 says death shall be no more. Many readers take Isaiah to be describing the world to come in the terms of his own day. Others, including some who expect a long age of blessing on earth before the end, take 65:20 as describing that earlier age. Faithful readers differ.
questions: What will no longer be heard in the new Jerusalem?
Which picture from chapter 11 comes back here?
How does the last verse of Isaiah differ in tone from the promise?

context: Mary is betrothed to Joseph and is found to be with child from the Holy Spirit. Joseph plans to end the betrothal quietly. An angel tells him in a dream to take Mary as his wife and to name the child Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins.
Matthew then speaks to the reader. All this took place to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet. He quotes Isaiah 7:14 and gives the meaning of Immanuel.
This is the first of many places where Matthew says that something happened to fulfill the Scriptures. He does not name Isaiah here, though he does elsewhere.

passages.text: All this took place to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet:
“Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Immanuel” (which means, God with us).

connections.text: Matthew writes that all this took place to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet, and then quotes Isaiah 7:14 (Matthew 1:22-23). The citation is explicit. Matthew reads 'they shall call his name Immanuel' where Isaiah reads 'shall call his name Immanuel', and Matthew adds the meaning of the name. In Isaiah 7 the sign is tied to a near event: before the boy knows how to refuse evil and choose good, the two kings Ahaz fears will be gone (7:16). Readers differ on whether a child in Isaiah's own day was a first stage of the sign. Matthew's claim about Jesus is plain either way.

nt: Matthew's Gospel ends the way it begins. The child called God with us says to his disciples, 'I am with you always, to the end of the age' (Matthew 28:20).
questions: Who does Matthew say was speaking through the prophet?
What word differs between Isaiah 7:14 and Matthew's quotation?
How does the name Immanuel fit what the angel says about the child?

context: John the Baptist has been arrested. Jesus withdraws to Galilee, leaves Nazareth, and makes his home in Capernaum by the Sea of Galilee. Matthew notes that this is the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali.
Those were the tribes Isaiah named. Matthew says Jesus' move fulfilled what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah, and he quotes the lines about Galilee of the Gentiles and the great light.
From that time Jesus begins to preach: repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand. The light Isaiah promised to the north arrives as a preacher.

passages.text: so that what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled:
the people dwelling in darkness have seen a great light, and for those dwelling in the region and shadow of death, on them a light has dawned.

connections.text: Matthew names the prophet Isaiah and quotes Isaiah 9:1-2 (Matthew 4:14-16). The wording shifts a little. Isaiah has 'The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light'. Matthew has 'the people dwelling in darkness have seen a great light'. Matthew quotes the light in Galilee. He does not quote the child of Isaiah 9:6-7. Christians read those verses of Jesus because of the quotation Matthew does make and because Gabriel promises Mary's son the throne of David (Luke 1:32-33).

nt: Matthew quotes only the opening of Isaiah's prophecy here. Jesus later says of himself, 'I am the light of the world' (John 8:12).
questions: Where does Jesus go to live, and whose old tribal lands are these?
Which verses of Isaiah 9 does Matthew quote, and which does he not?
What does Jesus begin to preach?

context: Jesus comes to Nazareth, where he had been brought up, and goes to the synagogue on the Sabbath as his custom was. He stands up to read, and the scroll of the prophet Isaiah is given to him.

He finds the place and reads about the Spirit of the Lord, good news to the poor, liberty to the captives, and the year of the Lord's favor. He rolls up the scroll, gives it back, and sits down. Every eye is fixed on him.

His sermon begins with one sentence: today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing. At first the people speak well of him. By the end of the visit they try to throw him off a cliff (4:28-30).

passages.text: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim liberty to the captives and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty those who are oppressed,
to proclaim the year of the Lord's favor.”
And he began to say to them, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.”

connections.text: Luke says Jesus was given the scroll of the prophet Isaiah and found the place where this was written, and Jesus then says, 'Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing' (Luke 4:17-21). The citation is explicit. The wording in Luke is not identical to the ESV of Isaiah 61. Luke does not have 'to bind up the brokenhearted'. Luke has 'recovering of sight to the blind' where Isaiah has 'the opening of the prison to those who are bound'. Luke also has 'to set at liberty those who are oppressed', which is close to a line in Isaiah 58:6. And the reading stops at 'the year of the Lord's favor', before Isaiah's next words, 'the day of vengeance of our God'. Many readers think Jesus stopped there on purpose. Luke does not say why.

nt: Luke has just told how the Holy Spirit came down on Jesus at his baptism (Luke 3:22) and how he returned to Galilee in the power of the Spirit (4:14). The reading in Nazareth explains what that anointing was for.
questions: Which book is Jesus handed?
What does he say about the passage after he sits down?
Compare Luke 4:19 with Isaiah 61:2. Where does the reading stop?

context: John has reached the end of Jesus' public ministry. He sums it up sadly: though Jesus had done so many signs before them, they still did not believe in him.

John says this fulfilled Isaiah 53:1, the prophet's own complaint that his message was not believed. Then he goes further. They could not believe, he says, and he quotes Isaiah 6:10 about blinded eyes and a hardened heart.

Verse 41 ties the two quotations together. Isaiah said these things because he saw his glory and spoke of him. The nearest glory in view is the vision of Isaiah 6, the Lord high and lifted up. John is telling his readers that the one Isaiah saw on the throne is the one who went to the cross.

passages.text: so that the word spoken by the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled: “Lord, who has believed what he heard from us, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?”
“He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, lest they see with their eyes, and understand with their heart, and turn, and I would heal them.”
Isaiah said these things because he saw his glory and spoke of him.

connections.text: John writes 'For again Isaiah said' and quotes Isaiah 6:10 (John 12:39-40). The wording differs. In Isaiah it is a command to the prophet: 'Make the heart of this people dull, and their ears heavy, and blind their eyes'. In John it is a statement: 'He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart'. John leaves out the ears. Then John says Isaiah said these things because he saw his glory and spoke of him (12:41). In John's telling, the glory Isaiah saw in the temple was the glory of Christ. That claim is John's own, and he makes it openly.

John says the unbelief of the crowd happened so that the word spoken by the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled, and he quotes Isaiah 53:1 (John 12:38). John's quotation begins with the word 'Lord', which is not in the ESV of Isaiah 53:1. Otherwise the two match closely.

nt: John's two quotations come from the two halves of Isaiah, chapter 6 and chapter 53, and he gives both to the one prophet Isaiah. Some readers also note that 'high and lifted up' describes both the Lord in Isaiah 6:1 and the servant in Isaiah 52:13, and that John speaks of Jesus being lifted up (John 12:32). John does not spell that link out, so it is an observation and not a claim of the text.
questions: What had the crowd seen, and how did they respond?
Which two chapters of Isaiah does John quote?
Whose glory does John say Isaiah saw?

context: An angel sends Philip to the desert road from Jerusalem to Gaza. There he meets a court official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who had come to Jerusalem to worship and is reading the prophet Isaiah in his chariot.

Philip asks whether he understands what he is reading. The man says he cannot unless someone guides him. The passage is Isaiah 53:7-8, the sheep led to the slaughter. His question is the right one: about whom does the prophet say this, about himself or about someone else?
Philip opens his mouth, and beginning with this Scripture he tells him the good news about Jesus. They come to water, the man asks to be baptized, and he goes on his way rejoicing.

passages.text: Now the passage of the Scripture that he was reading was this: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he opens not his mouth.
And the eunuch said to Philip, “About whom, I ask you, does the prophet say this, about himself or about someone else?”
Then Philip opened his mouth, and beginning with this Scripture he told him the good news about Jesus.

connections.text: Luke gives the passage the Ethiopian was reading, and it is Isaiah 53:7-8 (Acts 8:32-33). The wording differs from the ESV of Isaiah. Acts has 'Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter and like a lamb before its shearer is silent', where Isaiah has the lamb led to the slaughter and the sheep silent before its shearers. Acts has 'In his humiliation justice was denied him', where Isaiah has 'By oppression and judgment he was taken away'. The man asks who the prophet is speaking about. Philip begins with this Scripture and tells him the good news about Jesus (8:35). The identification is Philip's, and Luke records it as the answer.

nt: Isaiah 56:3-5 promises a name better than sons and daughters to eunuchs who hold fast to God's covenant. Acts does not quote that passage, but many readers notice that the first person Philip explains Isaiah to is a eunuch from a far country.
questions: What is the official reading, and what does he ask?
Where does Philip begin his answer?
What does the man do when he believes?

context: Peter is writing to Christians who suffer for doing good, and in this part of the letter he speaks to household servants with harsh masters. He points them to Christ, who suffered for them and left an example, so that they might follow in his steps.

The description of Christ is built from Isaiah 53. He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth. When he was reviled he did not revile in return. He bore our sins in his body on the tree. By his wounds you have been healed.

Peter ends with the sheep. You were straying like sheep, he says, but now you have returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls. The servant who suffered in the sheep's place is also their shepherd.

passages.text: He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth.
He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we might die to sin and live to righteousness. By his wounds you have been healed.
For you were straying like sheep, but have now returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls.

connections.text: Peter uses the words of Isaiah 53 without any phrase such as it is written. The source is not in doubt. 1 Peter 2:22 reads 'He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth', where Isaiah 53:9 reads 'although he had done no violence, and there was no deceit in his mouth'. 1 Peter 2:24 reads 'By his wounds you have been healed', where Isaiah 53:5 reads 'with his wounds we are healed'. 1 Peter 2:25 says you were straying like sheep, and Isaiah 53:6 says all we like sheep have gone astray. Peter changes we to you because he is speaking to his readers.

nt: Peter uses Isaiah 53 two ways at once. Christ's suffering is an example to follow, and it is a sacrifice no one else could make: he bore our sins. The second is the ground of the first.
questions: Who is Peter writing to in this part of the letter?
Which phrases here come from Isaiah 53?
What does Peter say Christ's death was for?

context: After the last judgment John sees a new heaven and a new earth. The holy city, new Jerusalem, comes down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.

A loud voice from the throne says that the dwelling place of God is with man. He will wipe away every tear from their eyes. Death, mourning, crying, and pain are gone, for the former things have passed away.
Then the one seated on the throne speaks: 'Behold, I am making all things new.' Isaiah heard God promise this. John sees it done.

passages.text: Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and the sea was no more.
He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away.
And he who was seated on the throne said, “Behold, I am making all things new.”

connections.text: This is shared wording and not a marked quotation. Revelation never introduces an Old Testament text with a phrase such as it is written. John sees 'a new heaven and a new earth' (Revelation 21:1), and Isaiah 65:17 promises 'new heavens and a new earth'. Revelation 21:4 says the former things have passed away, and Isaiah 65:17 says the former things shall not be remembered. Isaiah 65:19 promises an end to the sound of weeping, and Revelation 21:4 says God will wipe away every tear. 2 Peter 3:13 says Christians are waiting for new heavens and a new earth according to his promise, which points back to a promise like this one.

nt: Revelation is full of Old Testament wording but never introduces it with a citation. Besides Isaiah 65:17, this passage also echoes Isaiah 25:8, where the Lord GOD swallows up death forever and wipes away tears from all faces.
questions: What does the voice from the throne say about where God lives?
What is gone from the new creation?
Which words here do you also find in Isaiah 65?

context: The book calls itself the revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to show his servants what must soon take place (1:1). John writes as a brother and partner in the tribulation, on the island of Patmos on account of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus (1:9).

What he sees first is Jesus. He wears a long robe and a golden sash. His eyes are like a flame of fire, his voice like the roar of many waters. He holds seven stars in his right hand, and a sharp two-edged sword comes from his mouth. He stands among seven lampstands, which he says are the seven churches. The risen Christ is in the middle of his churches.

Interpretation: the book says its message concerns what must soon take place and that the time is near (1:1, 1:3). Readers who think most of the book was fulfilled in the first century lean on those words. Others note that the book runs on to the last judgment and the new creation, and take soon to mean that the last days began with Christ's first coming. How the whole book is read turns partly on this.

passages.text: Behold, he is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him, even those who pierced him, and all tribes of the earth will wail on account of him. Even so. Amen.
Fear not, I am the first and the last, and the living one. I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades.

connections.text: The risen Christ tells John to write what he sees in a book and send it to the seven churches, and he names them (1:11). He explains that the seven lampstands are the seven churches (1:20). The first letter then begins, 'To the angel of the church in Ephesus write' (2:1). The text itself carries the reader from the vision to the letters.

This is shared wording and not a marked quotation. Revelation 1:7 says, 'Behold, he is coming with the clouds', and Daniel 7:13 has one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven. John sees 'one like a son of man' (1:13), the same phrase. There is a difference worth noticing. In Daniel it is the Ancient of Days whose hair is like pure wool (7:9). In Revelation the son of man has hair 'white, like white wool, like snow' (1:14). Jesus applied Daniel 7:13 to himself before the high priest (Matthew 26:64), so reading Daniel's son of man as Christ rests on his own words.

nt: John had seen something of this glory before, on the mountain where Jesus was transfigured and his face shone like the sun (Matthew 17:2). Revelation 1:7 joins Daniel 7:13 with Zechariah 12:10, the one whom they have pierced. Jesus joined the same two passages in Matthew 24:30.
questions: Why is John on Patmos?
Where is Jesus standing, and what do the lampstands stand for?
What does Jesus say about himself when John falls down?

context: The seven churches were in real cities, and the list makes a rough circle on the map: Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea. Each letter follows a pattern. Jesus describes himself, says 'I know', gives praise or blame, calls for a response, and makes a promise to the one who conquers.

The churches are a mixed group. Ephesus is sound in doctrine but has left its first love. Smyrna is poor and about to suffer, and receives no rebuke. Pergamum and Thyatira tolerate false teaching. Sardis has a name for being alive and is dead. Philadelphia has little power and has kept Christ's word. Laodicea is lukewarm and thinks it needs nothing.

Every letter ends with 'what the Spirit says to the churches', in the plural. Each church was meant to read the others' mail, and so are we. Interpretation: some have read the seven letters as seven periods of church history. Nothing in the text says so, and this map does not follow that reading.

passages.text: But I have this against you, that you have abandoned the love you had at first.
Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life.
Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and eat with him, and he with me.

connections.text: The risen Christ tells John to write what he sees in a book and send it to the seven churches, and he names them (1:11). He explains that the seven lampstands are the seven churches (1:20). The first letter then begins, 'To the angel of the church in Ephesus write' (2:1). The text itself carries the reader from the vision to the letters.

After the last letter John writes, 'After this I looked, and behold, a door standing open in heaven', and the voice says, 'Come up here, and I will show you what must take place after this' (4:1). That is the order of the visions. Readers differ on how the order of the visions relates to the order of events in history.

nt: Several of these churches appear elsewhere in the New Testament. Paul taught in Ephesus for two years (Acts 19:10) and wrote of the church in Laodicea (Colossians 4:13-16). Lydia, the first believer in Philippi, came from Thyatira (Acts 16:14).
questions: What words does Jesus use at the start of his message to each church?
Which two churches receive no rebuke, and what are they like?
What is promised to the one who conquers?

context: Chapter 4 is the first thing John is shown after the letters. He does not start with the dragon or the beast. He starts with a throne and one seated on it, who has the appearance of jasper and carnelian. The word throne comes up again and again in this chapter.

Around the throne are twenty-four elders on thrones, in white with golden crowns. Before it burn seven torches of fire. Four living creatures, full of eyes, say day and night that the Lord God Almighty is holy. The elders cast their crowns before the throne and say that God is worthy, because he created all things.

Interpretation: John does not explain the twenty-four elders. Many readers take them to stand for the whole people of God, twelve tribes and twelve apostles together, as on the gates and foundations of the city in 21:12-14. Others take them as an order of angels. The text does not say.

passages.text: At once I was in the Spirit, and behold, a throne stood in heaven, with one seated on the throne.
Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come!
Worthy are you, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honor and power, for you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created.

connections.text: After the last letter John writes, 'After this I looked, and behold, a door standing open in heaven', and the voice says, 'Come up here, and I will show you what must take place after this' (4:1). That is the order of the visions. Readers differ on how the order of the visions relates to the order of events in history.

Chapters 4 and 5 are one scene. Chapter 5 begins, 'Then I saw in the right hand of him who was seated on the throne a scroll'. The Lamb appears beside the same throne and takes the scroll from the right hand of the one seated on it (5:6-7).

This is shared wording and not a marked quotation. Both prophets see a throne with four living creatures. The four faces are the same: a man, a lion, an ox, and an eagle (Ezekiel 1:10 and Revelation 4:7). Both see something like crystal near the throne (Ezekiel 1:22 and Revelation 4:6) and a brightness like a rainbow around it (Ezekiel 1:28 and Revelation 4:3). The differences are real too. In Ezekiel each creature has all four faces and four wings. In Revelation each creature has one of the faces and six wings, and they sing holy, holy, holy, which is like the seraphim of Isaiah 6:2-3. John's vision draws on both prophets.

nt: The song of the living creatures echoes the song of the seraphim in Isaiah 6:3. John's vision of the throne gathers up what Isaiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel each saw.
questions: What is the first thing John sees in heaven?
What do the living creatures say, and how often?
What reason do the elders give for worshiping God?

context: The one on the throne holds a scroll written on both sides and sealed with seven seals. A strong angel asks who is worthy to open it. No one in heaven or on earth or under the earth can, and John weeps loudly. The scroll is not explained in so many words. Most readers take it as God's purpose for judgment and salvation, which cannot go forward until someone worthy opens it.

One of the elders tells John to stop weeping. The Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered. John turns to look at the Lion and sees a Lamb, standing as though it had been slain. He hears of a Lion and sees a Lamb. The conquering was done by dying.

The Lamb takes the scroll, and worship spreads outward in rings. The living creatures and elders sing a new song. Then come countless angels, and then every creature in heaven and on earth. The Lamb receives the same worship as the one who sits on the throne.

passages.text: And one of the elders said to me, “Weep no more; behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered, so that he can open the scroll and its seven seals.”

And between the throne and the four living creatures and among the elders I saw a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain, with seven horns and with seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent out into all the earth.
Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honor and glory and blessing!

connections.text: Chapters 4 and 5 are one scene. Chapter 5 begins, 'Then I saw in the right hand of him who was seated on the throne a scroll'. The Lamb appears beside the same throne and takes the scroll from the right hand of the one seated on it (5:6-7).
The Lamb is declared worthy to open the seals (5:9), and chapter 6 begins, 'Now I watched when the Lamb opened one of the seven seals'. The same scroll and the same Lamb link the two chapters.

This line is marked interpretive. Revelation 5 does not mention the Passover. It shows a Lamb that was slain, whose blood ransoms a people and makes them a kingdom and priests (5:9-10). That is the pattern of the exodus: a lamb's blood, a people set free, and then 'a kingdom of priests' (Exodus 19:6). That Christ is the Passover lamb is stated outright elsewhere in the New Testament: 'Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed' (1 Corinthians 5:7). So the link between the Passover and Christ is explicit in Paul. Reading the Lamb of Revelation 5 as the Passover lamb in particular is an inference. Many readers also hear Isaiah 53:7, the lamb led to the slaughter.

This is shared wording and not a marked quotation. Zechariah is told that the seven lamps 'are the eyes of the LORD, which range through the whole earth' (4:10). John sees the Lamb 'with seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent out into all the earth' (5:6). Seven eyes that go through all the earth appear in both. In Zechariah they are the LORD's. In Revelation they belong to the Lamb.

nt: John the Baptist called Jesus the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29). Peter says believers were ransomed with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Peter 1:18-19). Revelation uses the name Lamb for Jesus far more than any other book.
questions: Why does John weep?
What does he hear about, and what does he see?
What reason does the new song give for the Lamb being worthy?

context: As the Lamb opens the first four seals, four horses ride out: white, red, black, and pale. Their riders bring conquest, the taking of peace from the earth, scarcity, and death. The fifth seal shows the souls of those killed for the word of God, under the altar, asking how long. They are given white robes and told to rest a little longer.

The sixth seal shakes the whole creation. The sun turns black, the stars fall, and the sky is rolled up like a scroll. Kings and slaves alike hide in caves and call on the mountains to hide them from the wrath of the Lamb. The seventh seal brings silence in heaven (8:1).

Interpretation: faithful readers place the seals differently. Some see the wars and famines that led up to the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70. Many Reformed readers see the troubles that mark the whole age between Christ's two comings, much as Jesus describes in Matthew 24:6-8, with the sixth seal bringing us to the last day. Others place them in a final period just before Christ returns. Readers also differ on the rider of the white horse. Some take him as Christ or the advance of the gospel, and others as conquest or a false christ. Whichever reading is right, the seals are opened by the Lamb. Nothing in them is outside his hand.

passages.text: O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?
for the great day of their wrath has come, and who can stand?

connections.text: The Lamb is declared worthy to open the seals (5:9), and chapter 6 begins, 'Now I watched when the Lamb opened one of the seven seals'. The same scroll and the same Lamb link the two chapters.

The sixth seal ends with a question, 'who can stand?' (6:17). Chapter 7 follows with 'After this I saw', and shows the servants of God sealed and a great multitude standing before the throne (7:9). The seventh seal is not opened until 8:1. The question and its answer sit next to each other in the text.

When the Lamb opens the seventh seal there is silence in heaven, and then John sees seven angels who are given seven trumpets (8:1-2). The trumpets come out of the last seal in John's telling. Interpretation: some readers take the trumpets as later events than the seals. Others take them as a second look at the same period, since both series end with the last day (6:12-17 and 11:15-18).

nt: Zechariah also saw horses of different colors sent out through the earth (Zechariah 1:8-11 and 6:1-8). That passage is in a different chapter from the lampstand stop on this map. The list of troubles is close to what Jesus foretold in Matthew 24:6-8: wars, famines, and earthquakes, which he calls the beginning of the birth pains.
questions: Who opens each seal?
What do the martyrs ask, and what are they given?
What question ends the chapter?

context: Chapter 6 ended by asking who can stand on the day of wrath. Chapter 7 answers before the last seal is opened. Four angels hold back the winds until the servants of God are sealed on their foreheads. John hears the number: 144,000, twelve thousand from each of twelve tribes.

Then he looks and sees a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, tribe, people, and language. They stand before the throne in white robes with palm branches, crying that salvation belongs to God and to the Lamb. An elder explains that they have come out of the great tribulation and have washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb.

Interpretation: many Reformed readers take the 144,000 and the great multitude as the same people seen two ways, the whole church counted and kept by God on earth and then safe before the throne. They note that John hears one thing and sees another, as he heard of a Lion and saw a Lamb in chapter 5. Other readers take the 144,000 as believers from the tribes of Israel and the multitude as believers from the nations. Readers also differ on whether the great tribulation is one final period or the suffering of the church through the whole age.

passages.text: After this I looked, and behold, a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, clothed in white robes, with palm branches in their hands,
These are the ones coming out of the great tribulation. They have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.
For the Lamb in the midst of the throne will be their shepherd, and he will guide them to springs of living water, and God will wipe away every tear from their eyes.

connections.text: The sixth seal ends with a question, 'who can stand?' (6:17). Chapter 7 follows with 'After this I saw', and shows the servants of God sealed and a great multitude standing before the throne (7:9). The seventh seal is not opened until 8:1. The question and its answer sit next to each other in the text.

nt: The promises at the end of this chapter come back in chapter 21: God shelters his people, and every tear is wiped away. The words draw on Isaiah 49:10 and 25:8. A crowd no one can count, from every nation, also recalls God's promise to Abraham of offspring like the stars, in whom all nations would be blessed (Genesis 22:17-18).
questions: What question from chapter 6 does this chapter answer?
What does John hear, and what does he then see?
How did the robes become white?

context: The prayers of the saints rise before God with incense, and then the trumpets begin. Hail and fire, the sea turned to blood, bitter waters, and darkness strike a third of the earth. They recall the plagues on Egypt (Exodus 7 to 10). They are warnings, and they are limited. The fifth and sixth trumpets are worse, and still the rest of mankind does not repent (9:20-21).

Before the seventh trumpet there is an interlude, as there was before the seventh seal. John eats a little scroll and is told to prophesy again. Two witnesses prophesy in sackcloth for 1,260 days. The beast kills them, the world celebrates, and after three and a half days God raises them and calls them up to heaven.

The seventh trumpet brings the end: the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and the time has come for the dead to be judged (11:15-18). Interpretation: because this series reaches the last judgment in chapter 11, and the story then seems to start again in chapter 12, many Reformed readers think Revelation tells of the same period several times from different sides. William Hendriksen set this reading out in his book More Than Conquerors. Others read the seals, trumpets, and bowls as one sequence of events, each following the last.

passages.text: The rest of mankind, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent of the works of their hands nor give up worshiping demons and idols of gold and silver and bronze and stone and wood, which cannot see or hear or walk,
These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth.
The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever.

connections.text: When the Lamb opens the seventh seal there is silence in heaven, and then John sees seven angels who are given seven trumpets (8:1-2). The trumpets come out of the last seal in John's telling. Interpretation: some readers take the trumpets as later events than the seals. Others take them as a second look at the same period, since both series end with the last day (6:12-17 and 11:15-18).

This is shared wording and not a marked quotation. Of the two witnesses John is told, 'These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth' (11:4). Zechariah sees two olive trees beside the lampstand and is told, 'These are the two anointed ones who stand by the Lord of the whole earth' (4:14). In Zechariah there is one lampstand, and in Revelation there are two. Who the two witnesses are is a matter of interpretation. Many Reformed readers take them as the witnessing church. Others expect two individual prophets.

nt: Paul also speaks of a trumpet at which the dead are raised, and in 1 Corinthians 15:52 he calls it the last trumpet (see also 1 Thessalonians 4:16). Whether that is the same as John's seventh trumpet is something readers discuss, and the text does not say.
questions: How much of the earth do the first trumpets strike, and what does that suggest?
How do people respond to the warnings?
What is announced when the seventh trumpet sounds?

context: John calls this a great sign. A woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet and a crown of twelve stars, cries out in birth pains. A great red dragon with seven heads and ten horns stands in front of her, to devour her child the moment he is born.

She gives birth to a male child who is to rule all the nations with a rod of iron, and the child is caught up to God and to his throne. The words about the rod of iron come from Psalm 2:9, a psalm about the LORD's anointed king. War breaks out in heaven. Michael and his angels fight the dragon, and the dragon is thrown down to the earth. A loud voice says that the accuser of the brothers has been thrown down, and that they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb.

Interpretation: nearly all readers take the child as Christ, and the catching up as his ascension, with his whole earthly life passed over in a single line. The woman is most often taken as the people of God, from whom Christ came and who are then persecuted. Her sun, moon, and twelve stars recall Joseph's dream about the family of Israel (Genesis 37:9). Roman Catholic readers have often seen Mary here. The 1,260 days in the wilderness (12:6) are taken by some as an exact three and a half years near the end, and by others as a figure for the whole time of the church's trial. The dragon is not open to dispute. John names him in verse 9.

passages.text: She gave birth to a male child, one who is to rule all the nations with a rod of iron, but her child was caught up to God and to his throne,
And they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death.

connections.text: The dragon goes off to make war on the rest of the woman's offspring and stands on the sand of the sea (12:17). John then sees a beast rising out of the sea, and 'to it the dragon gave his power and his throne and great authority' (13:2). The text names the dragon as the power behind the beast.

This line is marked interpretive. Revelation 12:9 says in plain words that the dragon is 'that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan'. So the text itself identifies the serpent. It also speaks of a woman, her child, and 'the rest of her offspring' (12:17), with the serpent at war against them, which is the shape of Genesis 3:15. But Revelation does not quote Genesis 3:15 or say that the promise is fulfilled here. Reading chapter 12 as the outworking of that promise is the common Reformed reading, and it is a reading. Paul echoes the same promise in Romans 16:20: the God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet.

nt: Jesus spoke of his death as the casting out of the ruler of this world (John 12:31), and he told the seventy-two that he saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven (Luke 10:18). The dragon is furious because he has lost, and he knows that his time is short (12:12).
questions: What does the dragon want to do, and does he succeed?
Who does John say the dragon is?
By what do the believers conquer him?

context: The first beast rises from the sea with ten horns and seven heads. It looks like a leopard, a bear, and a lion together, and the dragon gives it his power and throne. One of its heads seems to have a mortal wound that has healed. The whole earth marvels and worships it, asking who can fight against it. It is allowed to make war on the saints for forty-two months.

The second beast rises from the earth. It has two horns like a lamb and speaks like a dragon. It performs signs, makes the earth worship the first beast, and lets no one buy or sell without the mark of the beast's name or number. Later it is called the false prophet (19:20). John says the number is the number of a man, and the number is 666.

Interpretation: many readers take the first beast as the Roman empire, which demanded worship of its emperors in John's day, and the second as the local powers that enforced that worship in Asia. Many of the Reformers applied these pictures to the papacy of their own time. Others take the beasts as state power and false religion wherever they join against Christ's people, in every age. Others expect a last personal Antichrist and a false prophet shortly before Christ returns. Many readers hold more than one of these together. As for 666, a common suggestion is that it adds up the letters of Nero Caesar written in Hebrew. Another is that six, one short of seven, three times over, stands for what always falls short of God. No reading is certain. John's own application is plain: here is a call for the endurance and faith of the saints.

passages.text: And the beast that I saw was like a leopard; its feet were like a bear's, and its mouth was like a lion's mouth. And to it the dragon gave his power and his throne and great authority.
Here is a call for the endurance and faith of the saints.

connections.text: The dragon goes off to make war on the rest of the woman's offspring and stands on the sand of the sea (12:17). John then sees a beast rising out of the sea, and 'to it the dragon gave his power and his throne and great authority' (13:2). The text names the dragon as the power behind the beast.

The woman called Babylon is 'sitting on a scarlet beast that was full of blasphemous names, and it had seven heads and ten horns' (17:3). The beast from the sea in 13:1 has ten horns and seven heads and blasphemous names on its heads. John presents the same beast in both chapters.

This is shared wording and not a marked quotation. Daniel sees four beasts come up out of the sea: one like a lion, one like a bear, one like a leopard, and a fourth with ten horns (7:3-7). John sees one beast rise out of the sea with ten horns, 'like a leopard; its feet were like a bear's, and its mouth was like a lion's mouth' (13:1-2). John's one beast carries the features of Daniel's four. In both books the beast has a mouth that speaks great things and makes war on the saints (Daniel 7:8, 21 and Revelation 13:5-7). Daniel is told that the four beasts are four kings (7:17). Which kingdoms they are, and what John's beast stands for, are matters of interpretation.

nt: John's letters say that antichrist is coming and that many antichrists have already come (1 John 2:18). Paul writes of a man of lawlessness who exalts himself (2 Thessalonians 2:3-4). How those passages fit with the beasts of Revelation 13 is one of the questions on which readers differ.
questions: Where does the first beast get its power?
What does the second beast make people do?
What does John call the saints to in verse 10?

context: One of the angels shows John the judgment of the great prostitute. She sits on a scarlet beast, dressed in purple and scarlet and gold, holding a golden cup. On her forehead is the name Babylon the great. She is drunk with the blood of the saints and the martyrs of Jesus.

Chapter 18 is her funeral song. An angel cries that Babylon the great has fallen. A voice calls God's people to come out of her. Kings, merchants, and sea captains stand far off and mourn, because in a single hour all her wealth is laid waste. The list of her cargo ends with slaves, that is, human souls (18:13).

Interpretation: the angel says the seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman sits, and that she is the great city that has dominion over the kings of the earth (17:9, 17:18). Most readers therefore see Rome, the city on seven hills. Some who date the book before AD 70 see Jerusalem. Many Reformed readers take Babylon as the world in its wealth, pride, and hostility to God, of which Rome was the form John's readers knew, and which reappears in every age. Many of the Reformers applied it to papal Rome. The name itself comes from the Old Testament city that carried Judah into exile.

passages.text: And on her forehead was written a name of mystery: “Babylon the great, mother of prostitutes and of earth's abominations.”
Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great!
Come out of her, my people, lest you take part in her sins, lest you share in her plagues;

connections.text: The woman called Babylon is 'sitting on a scarlet beast that was full of blasphemous names, and it had seven heads and ten horns' (17:3). The beast from the sea in 13:1 has ten horns and seven heads and blasphemous names on its heads. John presents the same beast in both chapters.

Chapter 19 begins 'After this'. The crowd in heaven praises God because he has judged the great prostitute (19:2), and then announces that the marriage of the Lamb has come (19:7). The prostitute city and the Bride are set against each other on purpose.

nt: The cry that Babylon has fallen is first heard in Isaiah 21:9, and the call to come out of her echoes Jeremiah 51:45. Peter sends greetings from a church he describes as 'at Babylon' (1 Peter 5:13), which most readers take as a name for Rome. That is one reason many identify John's Babylon with Rome.
questions: How is the woman dressed, and what is she drunk with?
Who mourns when Babylon falls, and why?
What are God's people told to do?

context: The word Hallelujah appears in the New Testament only in this chapter, four times. Heaven praises God because his judgments are true and just. He has judged the great prostitute and avenged the blood of his servants.

Then the praise turns from a funeral to a wedding. The marriage of the Lamb has come, and his Bride has made herself ready. It was granted her to clothe herself with fine linen, bright and pure, and John is told that the fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints. Her clothing is something she wears and also something she was given.

John falls at the angel's feet to worship him and is stopped at once. The angel is a fellow servant. Worship God. The Bride is identified later in the book as the holy city, new Jerusalem, the wife of the Lamb (21:2, 21:9-10), which is the people of God.

passages.text: Let us rejoice and exult and give him the glory, for the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his Bride has made herself ready;
Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb.

connections.text: Chapter 19 begins 'After this'. The crowd in heaven praises God because he has judged the great prostitute (19:2), and then announces that the marriage of the Lamb has come (19:7). The prostitute city and the Bride are set against each other on purpose.

nt: Jesus compared the kingdom of heaven to a wedding feast a king gave for his son (Matthew 22:1-14). Paul says Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, to present her to himself in splendor, and he calls marriage a picture of Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:25-32). Isaiah 25:6-8 promises a feast for all peoples on the day God swallows up death.
questions: Why does heaven say Hallelujah?
Who is the Bride, and what is she wearing?
What happens when John tries to worship the angel?

context: John sees heaven opened. A white horse appears, and its rider is called Faithful and True. His eyes are like a flame of fire, as in chapter 1, and on his head are many crowns. He wears a robe dipped in blood, and his name is The Word of God.

The armies of heaven follow him in fine linen. From his mouth comes a sharp sword with which to strike down the nations, and he will rule them with a rod of iron. He treads the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty. The verses that follow show the beast and the false prophet captured and thrown into the lake of fire (19:19-20).

Interpretation: most readers, amillennial and premillennial alike, take this as the visible return of Christ at the end of the age. Some postmillennial readers take it as a picture of Christ conquering the nations through the preaching of his word in this present age, since his only weapon is the sword from his mouth. On either reading the rider is Jesus, and he wins.

passages.text: Then I saw heaven opened, and behold, a white horse! The one sitting on it is called Faithful and True, and in righteousness he judges and makes war.
On his robe and on his thigh he has a name written, King of kings and Lord of lords.

connections.text: This line is dashed because the join between chapter 19 and chapter 20 is the disputed point. Chapter 20 begins, 'Then I saw an angel coming down from heaven'. Historic premillennial readers take 'Then I saw' as the next event in time: Christ returns in chapter 19, and the thousand years follow. Amillennial and most postmillennial readers take it as the next vision, which goes back to the start of the gospel age, as chapter 12 went back to the birth of Christ. The words 'Then I saw' mark the order of the visions. They do not settle the order of the events.

nt: The rod of iron comes from Psalm 2:9, and the winepress from Isaiah 63:3. The name The Word of God recalls the opening of John's Gospel: In the beginning was the Word (John 1:1). Paul describes the Lord Jesus being revealed from heaven with his mighty angels (2 Thessalonians 1:7).
questions: What names does the rider have?
What is his weapon, and where does it come from?
Which details match the vision of Jesus in chapter 1?

context: The passage is short, ten verses, and it is the only place in the Bible that speaks of a thousand years in this way. An angel seizes the dragon, binds him, and shuts him in the bottomless pit so that he may not deceive the nations any longer. John sees thrones, and the souls of those beheaded for the testimony of Jesus. They come to life and reign with Christ a thousand years. This is called the first resurrection. When the thousand years end, Satan is released, gathers the nations for battle, and is thrown into the lake of fire.

Interpretation, the amillennial view: the thousand years is a symbolic number for the whole time between Christ's first coming and his return. Satan was bound by Christ's death and resurrection in the sense the passage names, 'that he might not deceive the nations any longer' (20:3), so the gospel now goes to all peoples (compare Matthew 12:29 and John 12:31-32). The first resurrection is the life of believers who have died and now reign with Christ in heaven, or on another form of the view, the new birth. Chapter 20 goes back to the beginning of the age, as chapter 12 did. Christ returns once, and the resurrection of all, the last judgment, and the new creation come together. Augustine taught a form of this view, and it is widely held in Reformed churches.

Interpretation, the postmillennial view: this view also places Christ's return after the thousand years. It differs in what it expects before he comes. Through the preaching of the gospel and the work of the Holy Spirit, the nations will largely be brought to faith, and there will be a long age of peace and righteousness on earth. Many who hold it take the number as a figure for a long time. They point to promises such as Psalm 72, Isaiah 2:2-4, Matthew 13:31-33, and 1 Corinthians 15:25. Many Puritans held this hope, and so did Jonathan Edwards and Charles Hodge.

Interpretation, the historic premillennial view: chapters 19 and 20 are read in order. Christ returns (19:11-16), believers are raised bodily in the first resurrection, and Christ reigns on the earth for the thousand years, which may be an exact number or a long time. Afterward Satan is released, the rest of the dead are raised, and the last judgment follows. Those who hold it note that the martyrs 'came to life' (20:4) and that the rest of the dead 'did not come to life' until the thousand years were ended (20:5), and they argue that the words should mean bodily resurrection both times. Early Christian writers such as Justin Martyr and Irenaeus held a form of this view, and so have some Reformed teachers.

A note on a fourth view: dispensational premillennialism is widely held among evangelical Christians. It keeps Israel and the church as two peoples with separate plans and usually places a rapture of the church before a seven year tribulation. Reformed churches have generally not accepted it, because they confess one people of God in one covenant of grace, so this map does not lay out its timeline.

What all three Reformed views share: Christ reigns now at the Father's right hand. Satan's defeat is certain. Jesus will return bodily and visibly. The dead will be raised, all people will be judged, and God will make all things new. The Westminster Standards teach these things and do not use the word millennium. Reformed teachers have held each of the three views.

passages.text: And he seized the dragon, that ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years,
They came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years.

Blessed and holy is the one who shares in the first resurrection! Over such the second death has no power, but they will be priests of God and of Christ, and they will reign with him for a thousand years.

connections.text: This line is dashed because the join between chapter 19 and chapter 20 is the disputed point. Chapter 20 begins, 'Then I saw an angel coming down from heaven'. Historic premillennial readers take 'Then I saw' as the next event in time: Christ returns in chapter 19, and the thousand years follow. Amillennial and most postmillennial readers take it as the next vision, which goes back to the start of the gospel age, as chapter 12 went back to the birth of Christ. The words 'Then I saw' mark the order of the visions. They do not settle the order of the events.

The text gives this order itself: 'when the thousand years are ended, Satan will be released' (20:7), he is defeated and thrown into the lake of fire (20:10), and 'Then I saw a great white throne' (20:11). All three millennial views agree that the last judgment comes after the thousand years.

nt: Readers on every side bring other passages to this one. John 5:25-29 speaks of an hour that is now here, when the dead hear the voice of the Son of God and live, and of an hour that is coming, when all who are in the tombs come out. 1 Corinthians 15:22-26 speaks of Christ reigning until he has put all his enemies under his feet, the last of which is death. Each view reads these passages a little differently. It is wise to hold your own view with humility and to treat Christians who hold another one as brothers and sisters.
questions: What is Satan prevented from doing while he is bound?
Who reigns with Christ, and what is said about the second death?
What do all three views agree will happen in the end?

context: John sees a great white throne and one seated on it. Earth and sky flee from his presence. All the dead stand before the throne, great and small. The sea gives up its dead, and so do Death and Hades. No one is missing.

Books are opened, and the dead are judged by what is written in them, according to what they have done. Another book is opened as well, the book of life. Death and Hades are thrown into the lake of fire, which is the second death, and so is anyone whose name is not found written in the book of life.

There are two kinds of books. The books of deeds show that God's judgment is just. The book of life, which Revelation elsewhere calls the book of life of the Lamb who was slain (13:8), shows that those who are saved are saved by him. All three millennial views place this judgment at the end.

passages.text: Then I saw a great white throne and him who was seated on it. From his presence earth and sky fled away, and no place was found for them.

And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne, and books were opened. Then another book was opened, which is the book of life. And the dead were judged by what was written in the books, according to what they had done.

connections.text: The text gives this order itself: 'when the thousand years are ended, Satan will be released' (20:7), he is defeated and thrown into the lake of fire (20:10), and 'Then I saw a great white throne' (20:11). All three millennial views agree that the last judgment comes after the thousand years.

At the great white throne 'earth and sky fled away, and no place was found for them' (20:11). The next vision begins, 'Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away' (21:1). The second statement picks up the first.

This is shared wording and not a marked quotation. In Daniel thrones are placed, the Ancient of Days takes his seat, 'the court sat in judgment, and the books were opened' (7:9-10). In Revelation John sees a great white throne and the dead standing before it, 'and books were opened' (20:12). The scene and the phrase are the same.

nt: Jesus says the Son of Man will sit on his glorious throne and separate all the nations as a shepherd separates sheep from goats (Matthew 25:31-32). Paul says we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10).
questions: Who stands before the throne?
What two kinds of books are opened?
What makes the difference for those who are not thrown into the lake of fire?

context: The first heaven and the first earth have passed away. John sees the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God. A loud voice from the throne says that the dwelling place of God is with man. This is the promise that runs through the whole Bible: they will be his people, and God himself will be with them.

Every tear is wiped away. Death, mourning, crying, and pain are no more. The one on the throne says he is making all things new, and that he will give to the thirsty from the spring of the water of life without payment.
