An angel then shows John the city as the Bride, the wife of the Lamb. Its gates bear the names of the twelve tribes and its foundations the names of the twelve apostles. It has no temple and needs no sun, for the glory of God gives it light and its lamp is the Lamb. Interpretation: Reformed readers generally understand the new heaven and new earth as this creation set free and renewed, as Romans 8:21 says, and not as a different world replacing it. Peter's language of the heavens passing away with a roar (2 Peter 3:10) leads some to stress the break more than the continuity.

passages.text: Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and the sea was no more.
Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God.
He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away.

connections.text: At the great white throne 'earth and sky fled away, and no place was found for them' (20:11). The next vision begins, 'Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away' (21:1). The second statement picks up the first.

The angel who shows John the holy city (21:9-10) goes on to show him the river: 'Then the angel showed me the river of the water of life' (22:1). The river flows through the middle of the street of the city. It is one vision.

This is shared wording and not a marked quotation. Isaiah 65:17 promises 'new heavens and a new earth', and John sees 'a new heaven and a new earth' (21:1). Isaiah says the former things shall not be remembered, and Revelation 21:4 says the former things have passed away. Isaiah 65:19 promises an end to the sound of weeping, and Revelation 21:4 says God will wipe away every tear. 2 Peter 3:13 says Christians are waiting for new heavens and a new earth according to his promise.

nt: Paul says the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption (Romans 8:21). Peter says we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells (2 Peter 3:13). The promise that God will dwell with his people and be their God runs from Leviticus 26:11-12 through Ezekiel 37:27 to this chapter.
questions: What comes down out of heaven?
What does the voice from the throne say about God and his people?
Why does the city need no temple and no sun?

context: The Bible began in a garden with a river and the tree of life (Genesis 2:9-10). After the fall, the way to that tree was guarded (Genesis 3:24). At the end the tree is in the middle of a city, on both sides of a river that flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb, and its leaves are for the healing of the nations.

No longer will there be anything accursed. God's servants will worship him. They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads. There will be no night, and they will reign forever and ever.

The book closes with warnings and invitations. Jesus says three times that he is coming soon. The Spirit and the Bride say, Come. Whoever is thirsty may take the water of life without price. John's last prayer is the church's prayer: Amen. Come, Lord Jesus.

passages.text: Then the angel showed me the river of the water of life, bright as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb
No longer will there be anything accursed, but the throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it, and his servants will worship him.
He who testifies to these things says, “Surely I am coming soon.” Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!

connections.text: The angel who shows John the holy city (21:9-10) goes on to show him the river: 'Then the angel showed me the river of the water of life' (22:1). The river flows through the middle of the street of the city. It is one vision.

This is shared wording and not a marked quotation. Ezekiel sees water flowing from the temple, with trees on both sides of the river that bear fresh fruit every month, and 'their leaves for healing' (47:12). John sees the river of the water of life with the tree of life on either side, 'yielding its fruit each month', and he adds, 'The leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations' (22:2). There are differences. In Ezekiel the water comes from the temple. In Revelation it comes from the throne of God and of the Lamb, and the city has no temple (21:22). Ezekiel sees many trees. John sees the tree of life, which goes back to Genesis 2:9. And John adds that the healing is for the nations.

nt: Jesus said that whoever is thirsty should come to him and drink, and that rivers of living water would flow from the one who believes (John 7:37-38). The invitation in Revelation 22:17 to take the water of life without price sounds like Isaiah 55:1.
questions: Where does the river come from?
What tree is here, and where did the Bible last show it?
What does Jesus promise at the end, and how does the church answer?

context: Daniel has this dream in the first year of Belshazzar, king of Babylon. The four winds stir up the great sea, and four beasts come out of it: one like a lion with eagle's wings, one like a bear, one like a leopard with four heads, and a fourth that is terrifying, with iron teeth and ten horns. A little horn comes up with a mouth speaking great things.

Then the scene changes to a courtroom. Thrones are placed, and the Ancient of Days takes his seat, his clothing white as snow. The court sits and the books are opened. The fourth beast is destroyed, and the others lose their dominion.

With the clouds of heaven comes one like a son of man. He is brought before the Ancient of Days and given dominion, glory, and a kingdom that all peoples will serve and that will never pass away. An angel explains that the four beasts are four kings, and that the saints of the Most High will receive the kingdom (7:17-18). Interpretation: the four kingdoms have most often been taken as Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, and Rome. Other readers count them differently.

passages.text: As I looked, thrones were placed, and the Ancient of Days took his seat; his clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool; his throne was fiery flames; its wheels were burning fire.
I saw in the night visions, and behold, with the clouds of heaven there came one like a son of man, and he came to the Ancient of Days and was presented before him.

And to him was given dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations, and languages should serve him; his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom one that shall not be destroyed.

connections.text: This is shared wording and not a marked quotation. Revelation 1:7 says, 'Behold, he is coming with the clouds', and Daniel 7:13 has one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven. John sees 'one like a son of man' (1:13), the same phrase. There is a difference worth noticing. In Daniel it is the Ancient of Days whose hair is like pure wool (7:9). In Revelation the son of man has hair 'white, like white wool, like snow' (1:14). Jesus applied Daniel 7:13 to himself before the high priest (Matthew 26:64), so reading Daniel's son of man as Christ rests on his own words.

This is shared wording and not a marked quotation. Daniel sees four beasts come up out of the sea: one like a lion, one like a bear, one like a leopard, and a fourth with ten horns (7:3-7). John sees one beast rise out of the sea with ten horns, 'like a leopard; its feet were like a bear's, and its mouth was like a lion's mouth' (13:1-2). John's one beast carries the features of Daniel's four. In both books the beast has a mouth that speaks great things and makes war on the saints (Daniel 7:8, 21 and Revelation 13:5-7). Daniel is told that the four beasts are four kings (7:17). Which kingdoms they are, and what John's beast stands for, are matters of interpretation.

This is shared wording and not a marked quotation. In Daniel thrones are placed, the Ancient of Days takes his seat, 'the court sat in judgment, and the books were opened' (7:9-10). In Revelation John sees a great white throne and the dead standing before it, 'and books were opened' (20:12). The scene and the phrase are the same.

nt: Son of Man is the name Jesus used most often for himself. At his trial he told the high priest, 'you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven' (Matthew 26:64). That is Jesus applying Daniel 7:13 to himself.
questions: Where do the beasts come from, and what are they?
What happens when the Ancient of Days takes his seat?
What is given to the one like a son of man, and for how long?

context: Ezekiel was a priest carried off to Babylonia with King Jehoiachin. In the fifth year of that exile, by the Chebar canal, the heavens were opened and he saw visions of God. Far from the temple, he might have thought God was far away too.

A stormy wind comes out of the north with flashing fire. In it are four living creatures, each with four faces and four wings, and beside each a wheel within a wheel, their rims full of eyes. They go wherever the spirit goes, without turning.

Over their heads is an expanse shining like crystal, and above it the likeness of a throne, and on the throne a likeness with a human appearance, bright as fire, with a brightness around him like a rainbow. Ezekiel piles up words such as likeness and appearance, because he is describing what cannot be described. When he sees it, he falls on his face.

passages.text: As for the likeness of their faces, each had a human face. The four had the face of a lion on the right side, the four had the face of an ox on the left side, and the four had the face of an eagle.

Like the appearance of the bow that is in the cloud on the day of rain, so was the appearance of the brightness all around. Such was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD. And when I saw it, I fell on my face, and I heard the voice of one speaking.

connections.text: This is shared wording and not a marked quotation. Both prophets see a throne with four living creatures. The four faces are the same: a man, a lion, an ox, and an eagle (Ezekiel 1:10 and Revelation 4:7). Both see something like crystal near the throne (Ezekiel 1:22 and Revelation 4:6) and a brightness like a rainbow around it (Ezekiel 1:28 and Revelation 4:3). The differences are real too. In Ezekiel each creature has all four faces and four wings. In Revelation each creature has one of the faces and six wings, and they sing holy, holy, holy, which is like the seraphim of Isaiah 6:2-3. John's vision draws on both prophets.

nt: John's throne vision in Revelation 4 uses Ezekiel's four living creatures, crystal, and rainbow. Like Ezekiel, John sees it while cut off from his people, on Patmos.
questions: Where is Ezekiel when he sees this, and why does that matter?
What four faces do the creatures have?
What does Ezekiel do when he sees the glory?

context: Nine plagues had fallen on Egypt, and Pharaoh still would not let Israel go. God announced a tenth: the death of every firstborn in the land. For Israel he provided a way of safety.

Each household was to take a lamb without blemish, a male a year old, and kill it at twilight. They were to put some of its blood on the two doorposts and the lintel of the house, roast the lamb, and eat it in haste, dressed for travel. Not one of its bones was to be broken (12:46).

That night the LORD struck the firstborn of Egypt and passed over the houses marked with blood. Israel walked out free. God told them to keep the day as a memorial feast forever, and to tell their children what it meant.

passages.text: Your lamb shall be without blemish, a male a year old. You may take it from the sheep or from the goats,
The blood shall be a sign for you, on the houses where you are. And when I see the blood, I will pass over you, and no plague will befall you to destroy you, when I strike the land of Egypt.

connections.text: This line is marked interpretive. Revelation 5 does not mention the Passover. It shows a Lamb that was slain, whose blood ransoms a people and makes them a kingdom and priests (5:9-10). That is the pattern of the exodus: a lamb's blood, a people set free, and then 'a kingdom of priests' (Exodus 19:6). That Christ is the Passover lamb is stated outright elsewhere in the New Testament: 'Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed' (1 Corinthians 5:7). So the link between the Passover and Christ is explicit in Paul. Reading the Lamb of Revelation 5 as the Passover lamb in particular is an inference. Many readers also hear Isaiah 53:7, the lamb led to the slaughter.

nt: Jesus was crucified at Passover. Paul writes, 'Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed' (1 Corinthians 5:7). John notes that the soldiers did not break Jesus' legs and says this fulfilled the Scripture that not one of his bones will be broken (John 19:36), which matches the rule for the Passover lamb in Exodus 12:46. The Westminster Confession names the paschal lamb among the ordinances that pointed forward to Christ.
questions: What kind of lamb was each household to choose?
What did God say he would do when he saw the blood?
Who in the New Testament calls Christ our Passover lamb?

context: About twenty years after the first exiles came home from Babylon, the temple was still unfinished. Zerubbabel the governor and Joshua the high priest led a small and discouraged people. In one night Zechariah was given a series of visions to strengthen them.

In this one he sees a lampstand all of gold with seven lamps, and two olive trees beside it that supply it with oil. He asks what these are. The answer is a word for Zerubbabel: not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit. The great mountain in front of him will become a plain, and his hands will finish the house.

Whoever has despised the day of small things will rejoice. The seven lamps are the eyes of the LORD, which range through the whole earth. The two olive trees are the two anointed ones who stand by the Lord of the whole earth. Most readers take these as Zerubbabel and Joshua, the ruler and the priest, though the text does not name them.

passages.text: Then he said to me, “This is the word of the LORD to Zerubbabel: Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the LORD of hosts.
For whoever has despised the day of small things shall rejoice, and shall see the plumb line in the hand of Zerubbabel. “These seven are the eyes of the LORD, which range through the whole earth.”
Then he said, “These are the two anointed ones who stand by the Lord of the whole earth.”

connections.text: This is shared wording and not a marked quotation. Zechariah is told that the seven lamps 'are the eyes of the LORD, which range through the whole earth' (4:10). John sees the Lamb 'with seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent out into all the earth' (5:6). Seven eyes that go through all the earth appear in both. In Zechariah they are the LORD's. In Revelation they belong to the Lamb.

This is shared wording and not a marked quotation. Of the two witnesses John is told, 'These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth' (11:4). Zechariah sees two olive trees beside the lampstand and is told, 'These are the two anointed ones who stand by the Lord of the whole earth' (4:14). In Zechariah there is one lampstand, and in Revelation there are two. Who the two witnesses are is a matter of interpretation. Many Reformed readers take them as the witnessing church. Others expect two individual prophets.

nt: Revelation uses this vision more than once. Christ walks among seven golden lampstands, which are the seven churches (1:12-13, 1:20). The Lamb has seven eyes sent out into all the earth (5:6). The two witnesses are called the two olive trees and the two lampstands (11:4). In Revelation the lampstands are the churches, and their light depends on the Spirit, as it did in Zechariah.
questions: What is discouraging the people in Zechariah's day?
How does God say the work will be done?
What are the seven lamps said to be?

context: The serpent had tempted the woman, and she and her husband ate from the tree God had forbidden. When God comes to them, he questions the man and the woman, but he does not question the serpent. He curses it.

Within that curse is a promise. God himself will put enmity between the serpent and the woman, and between its offspring and hers. The conflict will end with a wound on each side: the serpent's head bruised, and the heel of the woman's offspring bruised.

Genesis does not say who the offspring is. Within Genesis the promise narrows, to Seth, to Abraham, and to Judah. Reformed teaching reads the verse as the first announcement of the gospel, and the Westminster Confession speaks of Christ as the seed of the woman who should bruise the serpent's head.

passages.text: I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring; he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel.

connections.text: This line is marked interpretive. Revelation 12:9 says in plain words that the dragon is 'that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan'. So the text itself identifies the serpent. It also speaks of a woman, her child, and 'the rest of her offspring' (12:17), with the serpent at war against them, which is the shape of Genesis 3:15. But Revelation does not quote Genesis 3:15 or say that the promise is fulfilled here. Reading chapter 12 as the outworking of that promise is the common Reformed reading, and it is a reading. Paul echoes the same promise in Romans 16:20: the God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet.

nt: The New Testament does not quote Genesis 3:15 directly. It does say that the Son of God appeared to destroy the works of the devil (1 John 3:8), that through death he destroyed the one who has the power of death (Hebrews 2:14), and that God will soon crush Satan under the feet of his people (Romans 16:20). Revelation twice calls the devil 'that ancient serpent' (12:9 and 20:2).
questions: Who puts the enmity between the serpent and the woman?
What happens to the serpent, and what happens to the woman's offspring?
What does Revelation 12:9 call the dragon?

context: Isaiah's book ends with the largest promise in it. God says he creates new heavens and a new earth. The word create is the word used in Genesis 1:1.

The former things, the troubles Isaiah has spent sixty-four chapters describing, will not be remembered or come into mind. God will rejoice in Jerusalem and be glad in his people. No more will the sound of weeping be heard in it, or the cry of distress.
The Isaiah map has this passage as its last stop and follows the rest of the chapter. Here it stands as the root of John's last vision.

passages.text: For behold, I create new heavens and a new earth, and the former things shall not be remembered or come into mind.
I will rejoice in Jerusalem and be glad in my people; no more shall be heard in it the sound of weeping and the cry of distress.

connections.text: This is shared wording and not a marked quotation. Isaiah 65:17 promises 'new heavens and a new earth', and John sees 'a new heaven and a new earth' (21:1). Isaiah says the former things shall not be remembered, and Revelation 21:4 says the former things have passed away. Isaiah 65:19 promises an end to the sound of weeping, and Revelation 21:4 says God will wipe away every tear. 2 Peter 3:13 says Christians are waiting for new heavens and a new earth according to his promise.

nt: Peter writes that according to his promise we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells (2 Peter 3:13). The promise he has in mind is this one, or Isaiah 66:22, which repeats it.
questions: What does God say he will create?
What will happen to the former things?
What sound will no longer be heard?

context: Ezekiel's last nine chapters are a vision of a new temple, given in the twenty-fifth year of the exile, when the first temple lay in ruins. In chapter 43 the glory of the LORD, which Ezekiel had seen leave, comes back to fill the house.

Then a guide brings him to the door of the temple, and water is coming out from under the threshold. A thousand cubits on it is ankle deep, then knee deep, then waist deep, and then a river that cannot be crossed. The text names no stream flowing into it. It grows as it goes.

It runs east and down into the Dead Sea, and the salt water becomes fresh. There are fish of every kind, and fishermen spread their nets. On both banks grow trees whose leaves do not wither and whose fruit does not fail, because the water for them flows from the sanctuary. Interpretation: readers differ on how Ezekiel's temple vision is to be fulfilled. Reformed readers generally take it as a picture, in the terms of Ezekiel's own day, of the life that flows from God's presence, which the New Testament finds in Christ and in the new creation. They do not expect a future building.

passages.text: And wherever the river goes, every living creature that swarms will live, and there will be very many fish. For this water goes there, that the waters of the sea may become fresh; so everything will live where the river goes.

And on the banks, on both sides of the river, there will grow all kinds of trees for food. Their leaves will not wither, nor their fruit fail, but they will bear fresh fruit every month, because the water for them flows from the sanctuary. Their fruit will be for food, and their leaves for healing.

connections.text: This is shared wording and not a marked quotation. Ezekiel sees water flowing from the temple, with trees on both sides of the river that bear fresh fruit every month, and 'their leaves for healing' (47:12). John sees the river of the water of life with the tree of life on either side, 'yielding its fruit each month', and he adds, 'The leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations' (22:2). There are differences. In Ezekiel the water comes from the temple. In Revelation it comes from the throne of God and of the Lamb, and the city has no temple (21:22). Ezekiel sees many trees. John sees the tree of life, which goes back to Genesis 2:9. And John adds that the healing is for the nations.

nt: Jesus stood up at a feast in Jerusalem and said that rivers of living water would flow from the one who believes in him, and John explains that he said this about the Spirit (John 7:37-39). Revelation 22:1-2 shows the river itself, flowing from the throne.
questions: Where does the water come from?
What happens to the Dead Sea when the river reaches it?
What are the fruit and the leaves of the trees for?

context: This week walks the promise from its first wide form to a family, and then to the night the child is born. It starts in the garden, after sin. It moves to Abraham on the mountain. It ends in Bethlehem, where angels call the baby Savior and Lord.

You are watching one hope become clearer. First a child of the woman. Then Abraham's offspring, who will bless the nations. Then a birth in the city of David. Not every step has a single verse that says, this is the next chapter. The New Testament does say the offspring is Christ, and that God's Son was born of a woman.
Read it slowly. Notice which lines the New Testament draws in plain words, and which line is a faithful reading that the text itself does not spell out.

passages.text: he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel.
in your offspring shall all the nations of the earth be blessed
For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Savior, who is Christ the Lord.

connections.text: Between the garden and Abraham, the map draws a typology line. Some readers see the promised child narrowed to Abraham's line. Genesis does not state that join. Hold it as a careful reading, not as a quotation.
From Abraham the explicit line reaches Jesus. Paul says the offspring is Christ (Galatians 3:16), and Matthew calls him the son of Abraham (Matthew 1:1).

Galatians 4:4 explicitly says God's Son was born of woman. It does not quote Genesis 3:15 or label the birth its fulfillment. The Westminster Confession 8.6 identifies Christ as the woman's offspring, so this is a confessional Reformed reading rather than a direct fulfillment formula in Galatians.

nt: Taken together, the New Testament reads this week as promise and arrival. Galatians 3:16 identifies Abraham's offspring as Christ. Galatians 4:4 says the Son was born of woman. Matthew 1:1 sets Jesus in Abraham's family. Luke 2:11 announces the birth in David's city. Romans 16:20 speaks of Satan crushed, which many readers set beside the garden promise without claiming it is a direct quotation.
questions: Where does the promise get more specific this week?
Which connection is explicit, and which is typology?
What would you say the angel announces that the garden promise only hinted?

context: This week follows a king. Jacob gives the scepter to Judah. Isaiah sees a shoot from Jesse. God promises David a throne forever. The family line reaches Joseph. Gabriel tells Mary the throne is for her son. The child is born in David's town.

Some stops sit side by side without one verse joining them in a single sentence. Jesse and David are father and son in the story, and the promises belong to one royal family, even where the map has no separate line between two neighboring stops.
Listen for the word forever, and for the title son of David. Those are the notes that keep ringing until the birth.

passages.text: The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor the ruler’s staff from between his feet, until tribute comes to him; and to him shall be the obedience of the peoples.
And the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.

connections.text: The New Testament explicitly identifies Jesus with Judah and Jesse, and Matthew traces the genealogy to Joseph: Revelation 5:5, Hebrews 7:14, Romans 15:12, and Matthew 1:16. Calling Joseph's role legal fatherhood is a standard inference from the genealogy and naming, not Matthew's own phrase.
David's covenant reaches Gabriel's words in Luke 1:32-33. The New Testament speaks the forever throne over Mary's son.
David's house and Bethlehem belong together. Luke 2:4 calls the town the city of David, and the child of this week is born there.

nt: The New Testament reads this week as one royal story. Matthew 1 opens with the son of David and then lists the names. Luke's angel hands David's throne to Jesus. Paul uses Isaiah's root of Jesse for the hope of the nations. The king promised to Judah is not left in the past.
questions: Which family names does this week follow, in order?
Where does the angel sound most like 2 Samuel 7?
Why do Christian interpreters describe Joseph as Jesus' legal father, and what details in Matthew support that inference?

context: This week is about a sign and the people in it. Isaiah says a virgin will bear a son called Immanuel. Isaiah also says a child is born and a son is given. Then the story arrives at Mary, who hears Gabriel, and at Joseph, who obeys a dream. The week ends when the child is born.
The sign is not a trick. Matthew says the birth happened this way to fulfill the prophet. God with us is a person, conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of Mary, named by Joseph.

Hold Isaiah 9 carefully. Matthew quotes the light in Galilee from the start of that chapter. The government on the child's shoulder is in the rest of the same prophecy, read with the angel's promise of David's throne.

passages.text: Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.
“Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Immanuel” (which means, God with us).

connections.text: Isaiah's Immanuel and Mary's motherhood both meet the birth in explicit New Testament lines: Matthew 1:22-23 and Luke 2:7.
Gabriel's announcement is spoken to Mary. Luke 1:26-38 is that explicit sequence.

Matthew's genealogy reaches Joseph, calls him Mary's husband, and records that he named Jesus (Matthew 1:16, 20, 25). Christian interpreters commonly describe this as legal fatherhood, but Matthew does not use that phrase. The same chapter states the Spirit's conception.

nt: Matthew 1:22-23 is the New Testament's direct reading of Isaiah 7:14. He quotes it and translates Immanuel. Luke 1:31-35 tells Mary she will conceive by the Holy Spirit and bear a son named Jesus. Galatians 4:4 says the Son was born of woman. Those are the clear readings of this week's sign.
questions: What does Immanuel mean, and who tells you the meaning?
How do Mary's question and Joseph's dream fit together?
Which part of Isaiah 9 does Matthew quote, and which part do we connect by the angel's words?

context: This week is about a place. Micah says the ruler comes from little Bethlehem. The town already belongs to David and to Jesse. Wise men arrive asking for a king, and the teachers of Israel answer with Micah. The child is born there.
The smallness is part of the story. The prophet says the town is too little to count among the clans. God still chooses it.

passages.text: But you, O Bethlehem Ephrathah, who are too little to be among the clans of Judah, from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel
And you, O Bethlehem, in the land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for from you shall come a ruler who will shepherd my people Israel.

connections.text: Micah names the town, and Luke 2:4-7 tells the birth in it. Matthew 2:4-6 shows the scribes using the prophecy when Herod asks.
The wise men seek the child born king and worship him (Matthew 2:2, Matthew 2:11). That explicit line reaches Jesus.

nt: Matthew 2:4-6 is the New Testament reading of this week in one scene. The king is born. The rulers ask where. The Scriptures answer Bethlehem. Luke 2 simply narrates the journey and the birth. John 7:42 shows that people expected the Christ from David's village.
questions: Why does Micah call Bethlehem little, and how does Matthew's quotation speak of the town?
What question do the wise men ask in the capital?
Which line this week should you not treat as a Bible promise?

context: Christmas on this map is two stops. First the birth, in David's city, announced to shepherds. Then the person the birth reveals: Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham.
The day is not a pause in the story. It is the moment the promises become a baby you could hold. Savior, Christ, and Lord are angel words, not later nicknames.

There is no separate line drawn on the map from the birth straight to the title Jesus. The two stops belong together because the child who is born is that person. The lines into each stop, from Abraham, David, Isaiah, Micah, Mary, and the wise men, are what tie the night to the long story.

passages.text: For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Savior, who is Christ the Lord.
The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham.

connections.text: The birth gathers direct New Testament links from Immanuel in Matthew 1:22-23, from Mary in Luke 2:7, from Micah in Matthew 2:4-6, and from Bethlehem in Luke 2:4-7. Galatians 4:4 states that God's Son was born of woman. Reading that as the fulfillment of Genesis 3:15 is the confessional Reformed interpretation stated in Westminster Confession 8.6.

The person gathers direct New Testament lines from Abraham, Judah, Jesse, Isaiah's child, and the wise men. Matthew's genealogy also reaches Joseph, whose relationship to Jesus is explained in the Joseph note. Matthew 1:1 states the titles son of David and son of Abraham in one sentence.

nt: John 1:14 says the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. That is the Christmas fact in John's words. Luke 2:11 tells you what the angels called him. Matthew 1:1 tells you which promises he carries in his name. Read those three and the night is anchored.
questions: What titles does the angel use on the night of the birth?
What two family names does Matthew put on Jesus in his first verse?
Why can these two stops belong together even without one line drawn between them?

context: This path reads Deuteronomy from its first sentence to its last. Ten stops, in the order the book puts them.

It is one sermon, preached east of the Jordan by a man who knew he would not cross over. Moses goes back over the ten commandments, gives the command to love God with everything, explains the forty years in the desert, promises a prophet, calls a hanged man cursed, sets blessing and curse in front of the people, says the word is near, teaches them a song, and dies.

Four of the nine steps have no line between them, because Deuteronomy does not tie those chapters to each other in words. The lines this book does have mostly run out of it, to the writers who quote it. The second path follows those.

passages.text: Beyond the Jordan, in the land of Moab, Moses undertook to explain this law
I call heaven and earth to witness against you today, that I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse. Therefore choose life, that you and your offspring may live,
And there has not arisen a prophet since in Israel like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face

connections.text: Between the ten commandments and the command to love God, the link is in the text. Deuteronomy 6:1 points back to the commandment just given and says Moses was told to teach it.
Between the curses and the turn, the link is also in the text. Deuteronomy 30:1 names the blessing and the curse that had been set before them.

The one dashed line on this map runs from the end of the book back to the promise of a prophet. Deuteronomy 34:10 says no prophet like Moses has arisen since. Reading that as leaving the promise open is a careful reading, not something Deuteronomy states.

nt: The New Testament quotes this book often. Jesus uses it three times in the wilderness and once on the great commandment. Peter and Stephen quote the promise of a prophet. Paul quotes the curse, the hanged man, the word that is near, and the song. Walk the book first, and those quotations land differently.
questions: What is Moses doing in this book, and where is he standing?
Which stops on this path have no line between them, and why?
What has changed by the last stop that was not true at the first?

context: This path walks the places where the New Testament quotes Deuteronomy, with each Deuteronomy text set beside the writer who used it.

Twelve stops. Jesus tested in the wilderness, Jesus on the great commandment, Peter at the temple, Paul to the Galatians, Paul to the Romans. Most of the quotations are marked in the text itself, with it is written, or Moses said, or first Moses says. Two are not: Jesus gives Deuteronomy 6:5 as his own answer without a formula (Matthew 22:37), and Paul introduces Deuteronomy 30:14 only with 'But what does it say?' (Romans 10:8). In both the source is plain and undisputed. Nothing on this path rests on a guess about what a writer had in mind.

Watch the wording as you go. The New Testament writers generally quote the Old Testament in Greek, and words shift: the mouth of God for the mouth of the LORD, worship for fear, everyone and all added to the curse, the abyss for the sea. Matthew's mind for might is a change of a different kind. Deuteronomy 6:5 has heart, soul, and might, and Mark 12:30 has both mind and strength. Each stop says where a word moves and what the difference amounts to.

passages.text: Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God.
You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind.
The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart

connections.text: Two Deuteronomy chapters answer all three tests. Chapter 8 answers the bread, and chapter 6 answers the other two.
Paul quotes two Deuteronomy laws here, the last curse and the hanged man, and the path puts one on each side of him so you read the quotation between its two sources.
Romans 10 quotes Deuteronomy twice, chapter 30 and chapter 32, so this path sets it between those two stops as well.

nt: The order on this path is deliberate. Where a New Testament writer quotes two Deuteronomy texts, the writer stands between them. Galatians sits between the curse list and the hanged man. Romans sits between the word that is near and the song. That way the quotation is read with both of its sources in view.

context: This path reads Isaiah in the book's own order, sixteen stops from the opening charge to the new heavens and new earth. Isaiah preached in Jerusalem for about fifty years, under four kings, while the empire of Assyria swallowed the nations around Judah.

The first half of the path, through chapter 39, is set in those years. Isaiah sees the Lord, confronts King Ahaz, promises a royal child, and stands with King Hezekiah when the Assyrian army is at the wall. The second half, from chapter 40, speaks comfort to a people in exile in Babylon and beyond. It introduces the servant of the LORD, names Cyrus, and ends with a new creation.

Christians who hold that Isaiah wrote the whole book, as the New Testament's way of quoting it suggests, read the second half as prophecy given ahead of time. Many modern scholars assign chapters 40 to 66 to later writers. The timeline shows both views and says which one this map follows.

passages.text: Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory!
Comfort, comfort my people, says your God.
But he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed.

connections.text: The Immanuel sign and the Assyrian siege are joined by a place. Both scenes happen at the conduit of the upper pool.
The comfort of chapter 40 follows straight after the warning about Babylon in chapter 39. That is the hinge of the book.
The four servant passages are joined by dashed lines. Reading them as one figure is a common and old reading, but Isaiah does not number them or call them a set.

nt: Most stops on this path are quoted somewhere in the New Testament, but only some of those New Testament passages are stops on this map. Where a stop is quoted in a text the map does not hold, its Go deeper says where.
questions: What changes in the tone of the book at chapter 40?
Which stops are about a king, and which are about a servant?
How does the last stop answer the first?

context: This path sets passages from Isaiah beside New Testament writers who use them. There are thirteen stops: Matthew twice, Luke, John, Acts, Peter, and Revelation.

Six of the seven New Testament stops make their use of Isaiah plain. Matthew says it was to fulfill what was spoken. Jesus says today this Scripture has been fulfilled. John says Isaiah said. Luke tells us which passage the Ethiopian was reading. Peter uses the words of Isaiah 53 with no formula at all, and the source is not in doubt. The last stop is different. Revelation 21 shares Isaiah's wording without citing him, and the map marks that line as an echo.

Watch the wording as you go. The New Testament writers often quote the Old Testament in a form that differs a little from the ESV of Isaiah. Each stop says where a word moves. The notes state the difference and do not guess at the cause.

passages.text: All this took place to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet:
And he began to say to them, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.”
Isaiah said these things because he saw his glory and spoke of him.

connections.text: John quotes two Isaiah passages, chapter 6 and chapter 53, so the path puts him between those two stops.
Isaiah 53 is used by three New Testament stops in a row: John, Philip in Acts, and Peter.
The last line is an echo and not a citation. Revelation shares Isaiah's words about a new heaven and a new earth without naming him.

nt: The New Testament quotes Isaiah far more often than this path can show. Other well known places are Matthew 3:3 (Isaiah 40:3), Matthew 8:17 (Isaiah 53:4), Matthew 12:17-21 (Isaiah 42:1-4), Acts 13:47 (Isaiah 49:6), and Romans 15:12 (Isaiah 11:10).
questions: What phrase marks the quotation at each stop, where there is one?
Which chapter of Isaiah is used most on this path?
Where does a word change between Isaiah and the writer quoting him, and does the meaning change with it?

context: This path follows John's visions in the order he tells them, sixteen stops from the risen Christ on Patmos to the river of life. John wrote to seven churches under pressure, some from persecution and some from comfort and compromise. The book was meant to be read aloud to them, and it promises a blessing to those who hear and keep it (1:3).

Revelation speaks in pictures. Lampstands are churches, and John tells us so. A Lamb with seven horns and seven eyes is Jesus. Numbers such as seven, twelve, and a thousand carry meaning. Almost all of the pictures come from the Old Testament, which is the best guide to them.

Interpretation: faithful readers have read the book as a whole in four broad ways. Some see most of it fulfilled in the first century, in the fall of Jerusalem or the troubles of Rome (often called preterist). Some see a map of church history from John's day to the end, as many of the Reformers did (historicist). Some place most of chapters 4 to 22 shortly before Christ returns (futurist). Some see pictures of the conflict between Christ and evil that hold true in every age (idealist). Many Reformed readers combine these. They also differ on whether the visions run in one line or go over the same ground several times. This path keeps John's order and says at each stop where readers part ways.

passages.text: Blessed is the one who reads aloud the words of this prophecy, and blessed are those who hear, and who keep what is written in it, for the time is near.
Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honor and glory and blessing!
He who testifies to these things says, “Surely I am coming soon.” Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!

connections.text: Chapters 4 and 5 are the center the rest of the book is seen from. Everything that follows comes out of the scroll the Lamb opens.
No line joins the seventh trumpet to the woman and the dragon. Chapter 11 reaches the last judgment, and chapter 12 goes back to the birth of Christ. Many readers think the book starts over here.
The line into the thousand years is dashed. Whether chapter 20 follows chapter 19 in time is the point on which the three views differ.

nt: Whatever view a reader takes of the details, the message of the book to the churches is plain, and it was plain to its first hearers. Jesus has died and is alive. He knows his churches. The powers that oppose him are real, and they lose. So hold fast, worship God alone, and wait for him.
questions: What does John see first, before any vision of trouble?
Which stops on this path show worship in heaven?
How does the last stop answer the garden at the start of the Bible?

context: This path sets visions from Revelation beside the Old Testament passages they draw on. There are sixteen stops. An Old Testament root comes first each time, followed by the vision or visions that use it.

Revelation never quotes the Old Testament with a phrase such as it is written. It does something different. It is soaked in Old Testament wording, and John expects his hearers to notice. So the lines on this path are mostly echoes: the same phrase or the same picture in both places. Each stop says exactly what is shared and what is different.

Two lines are dashed. Reading the Lamb of chapter 5 against the Passover, and reading the dragon's war of chapter 12 as the outworking of Genesis 3:15, are both common Reformed readings with good support elsewhere in the New Testament. But Revelation does not state either link in so many words, so the map marks them as interpretation.

passages.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, with the clouds of heaven there came one like a son of man, and he came to the Ancient of Days and was presented before him.
Behold, he is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him, even those who pierced him, and all tribes of the earth will wail on account of him. Even so. Amen.
The leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations.

connections.text: Daniel 7 stands first because it reaches three stops: the son of man in chapter 1, the beast from the sea in chapter 13, and the opened books in chapter 20.
The Lamb stands between two roots. The Passover is before him on the path, and Zechariah's seven eyes are after him.
The line from Genesis 3:15 to the dragon is dashed. John names the dragon as the ancient serpent. He does not quote the promise.

nt: The path shows how the Bible holds together. The serpent of the first book is thrown down in the last. The Lamb who was slain is on the throne, and Paul calls Christ our Passover lamb. The river Ezekiel saw and the new earth Isaiah heard promised are where the story ends.
questions: Which Old Testament book is used most on this path?
At each pair of stops, what wording is shared, and what is different?
Why are two of the lines dashed?
